Furthermore, we disentangle the joint and individual components of these subspaces to identify latent directions that enable local image manipulation. Once discovered, these directions can be applied to different images to produce semantically consistent edits, making our method suitable for practical applications. Experimental results on various datasets demonstrate that our method can produce semantic edits that are more localized and have better fidelity compared to the state-of-the-art.

papers.title: Physics Steering: Causal Control of Cross-Domain Concepts in a Physics Foundation Model
papers.research_question: Whether scientific foundation models learn abstract, domain-general representations of physical phenomena that can be causally manipulated via activation steering.
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that a physics foundation model learns linearly steerable representations of physical concepts (e.g., vorticity, diffusion, temporal progression), and that injecting these directions during inference enables fine-grained causal control over simulation behavior. The concept directions are domain-general and transfer across unrelated physical systems.
papers.conclusion: Interpretability techniques from LLMs can be successfully adapted to scientific foundation models, providing evidence that these models develop abstract, domain-general representations of fundamental physical concepts that are linearly encoded and causally steerable.
papers.key_findings:
Single directions in the model's activation space correspond to specific physical concepts like vorticity, diffusion, and simulation speed.
Injecting (adding or subtracting) these concept directions during inference causally steers model predictions, allowing induction or suppression of vortices, enhancement or suppression of diffusion, and speeding up or slowing down simulations.
The extracted concept directions transfer successfully between unrelated physical systems (e.g., from fluid dynamics to chemical reaction-diffusion), indicating they represent abstract, domain-general physical principles.
The results support the Linear Representation Hypothesis for scientific foundation models, showing physical concepts are represented linearly in activation space.
Steering effects are more physically plausible and interpretable when using spatially-averaged concept directions that discard spatial structure, compared to using full spatial tensors.
papers.limitation:
The physical plausibility of the steered results is an open question; including spatial dimensions in the steering tensor can lead to less physically realistic outcomes.
The effectiveness of steering depends on the initial conditions of the simulation; steering becomes more difficult and can produce distorted fields when the initial state is far from the target regime.
future_direction: Exploring the layer-dependence of concept representations and steering effects.
Further work to definitively assess the physicality and self-consistency of steered simulation results.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in mechanistic interpretability have revealed that large language models (LLMs) develop internal representations corresponding not only to concrete entities but also distinct, human-understandable abstract concepts and behaviour. Moreover, these hidden features can be directly manipulated to steer model behaviour. However, it remains an open question whether this phenomenon is unique to models trained on inherently structured data (ie. language, images) or if it is a general property of foundation models. In this work, we investigate the internal representations of a large physics-focused foundation model. Inspired by recent work identifying single directions in activation space for complex behaviours in LLMs, we extract activation vectors from the model during forward passes over simulation datasets for different physical regimes. We then compute "delta" representations between the two regimes. These delta tensors act as concept directions in activation space, encoding specific physical features. By injecting these concept directions back into the model during inference, we can steer its predictions, demonstrating causal control over physical behaviours, such as inducing or removing some particular physical feature from a simulation. These results suggest that scientific foundation models learn generalised representations of physical principles. They do not merely rely on superficial correlations and patterns in the simulations. Our findings open new avenues for understanding and controlling scientific foundation models and has implications for AI-enabled scientific discovery.

papers.title: Color encoding in Latent Space of Stable Diffusion Models
papers.research_question: How is color information encoded in the latent space of Stable Diffusion models, and how are color and shape representations disentangled?
papers.core_contribution: This work reveals that color information in Stable Diffusion is encoded along circular, opponent axes in latent channels c3 and c4, while intensity and shape are primarily in channels c1 and c2, indicating an interpretable structure aligned with efficient coding.
papers.conclusion: The analysis shows that color and shape are encoded in a partially disentangled manner in Stable Diffusion's latent space, with specific channels specializing in intensity, chromaticity, and shape, providing insights for future model understanding and editing applications.
papers.key_findings:
Color presents an opponent representation based on Black-White, Cyan-Magenta, and Orange-Blue channels in the latent space.
Chromatic information is mostly encoded in channel 3 (Cyan-Magenta) and channel 4 (Orange-Blue), with channel 4 entangled with shape.
Shape is mostly encoded in channel 1 (Black-White), but channels 2 and 4 also encode some shape information.
Channel 2 encodes low-frequency shape information.
The latent space exhibits a partially disentangled representation of color and shape across specific channels.
papers.limitation: Limitations in achieving fully disentangled representations due to standard training procedures on natural image data.
future_direction: Future work on conditioning generation based on latent representations
Improving editing applications for color and shape
Designing more disentangled generative frameworks
papers.abstract: Recent advances in diffusion-based generative models have achieved remarkable visual fidelity, yet a detailed understanding of how specific perceptual attributes - such as color and shape - are internally represented remains limited. This work explores how color is encoded in a generative model through a systematic analysis of the latent representations in Stable Diffusion. Through controlled synthetic datasets, principal component analysis (PCA) and similarity metrics, we reveal that color information is encoded along circular, opponent axes predominantly captured in latent channels c_3 and c_4, whereas intensity and shape are primarily represented in channels c_1 and c_2. Our findings indicate that the latent space of Stable Diffusion exhibits an interpretable structure aligned with a efficient coding representation. These insights provide a foundation for future work in model understanding, editing applications, and the design of more disentangled generative frameworks.

papers.title: FeatInv: Spatially resolved mapping from feature space to input space using conditional diffusion models
papers.research_question: How can we learn a high-fidelity, probabilistic mapping from spatially resolved feature maps to input space to improve feature space understanding in computer vision models?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes FeatInv, a method that uses a conditional diffusion model (ControlNet) to learn a high-fidelity, probabilistic mapping from spatially resolved feature maps to input space, enabling improved visualization and understanding of feature spaces in computer vision models.
papers.conclusion: FeatInv provides an effective probabilistic mapping from feature space to input space using a conditional diffusion model, enabling accurate and robust reconstruction across different model architectures and offering valuable applications for model interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
FeatInv can reconstruct high-fidelity natural images from feature maps of various models (ResNet50, ConvNeXt, SwinV2).
Using unpooled (spatially resolved) feature maps yields better reconstruction quality (higher cosine similarity and top5 match) and sample quality (lower FID) than using pooled feature maps.
The method is robust and generalizes across models (cross-model evaluation) and to out-of-distribution data (BAID dataset).
FeatInv enables applications such as FeatInv-Viz for visualizing concept steering in input space and investigating the composite nature of feature space via linear interpolations and spatial compositions.
Conditioning on earlier feature layers provides more detailed and accurate reconstructions, and the faithfulness of reconstruction extends beyond the specific layer used for conditioning.
papers.limitation:
Focuses exclusively on the domain of natural images.
Requires a pretrained diffusion model, which might not be readily available in all application contexts.
Every model and layer choice requires training a dedicated FeatInv model, representing a computational hurdle.
Application scenarios rely on modifications of the feature space, and there is a need for measures to detect input samples (feature maps) that are outside the scope of the model.
future_direction: Extend the approach to other domains, such as medical imaging.
Investigate finetuning to alleviate the need for training a model per layer.
Introduce measures to detect input samples (feature maps) that are outside the scope of the model.
papers.abstract: Internal representations are crucial for understanding deep neural networks, such as their properties and reasoning patterns, but remain difficult to interpret. While mapping from feature space to input space aids in interpreting the former, existing approaches often rely on crude approximations. We propose using a conditional diffusion model - a pretrained high-fidelity diffusion model conditioned on spatially resolved feature maps - to learn such a mapping in a probabilistic manner. We demonstrate the feasibility of this approach across various pretrained image classifiers from CNNs to ViTs, showing excellent reconstruction capabilities. Through qualitative comparisons and robustness analysis, we validate our method and showcase possible applications, such as the visualization of concept steering in input space or investigations of the composite nature of the feature space. This approach has broad potential for improving feature space understanding in computer vision models.

papers.title: Attribute Graphs Underlying Molecular Generative Models: Path to Learning with Limited Data
papers.research_question: How can we extract a graphical model (attribute graph) relating data attributes from the latent representations of a pre-trained generative model, and use this structure for robust prediction with limited out-of-distribution data?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes PerturbLearn, a method to extract an attribute graph (a DAG) from a pre-trained generative autoencoder by perturbing latent codes and observing influences on data attributes, and shows that using the Markov blanket from this graph for feature selection leads to robust prediction under distribution shifts with limited data.
papers.conclusion: The PerturbLearn framework successfully extracts a graphical model from a pre-trained generative model, and using this structure for feature selection enables more robust and generalizable predictors in scenarios with limited out-of-distribution data.
papers.key_findings:
The attribute graph derived by PerturbLearn captures latent-mediated influences among molecular attributes.
Predictors using the Markov blanket features from the PerturbLearn graph show better generalization and robustness to distribution shifts, especially when fine-tuning data is limited (e.g., n=7, 10, 25 samples).
The method is competitive with or outperforms existing causal discovery (GES, LiNGAM) and feature selection methods (Sparse Group Lasso, PPFS) in low-data regimes across multiple pharmacokinetic property prediction tasks.
The derived graphical model provides a means for sample-efficient domain adaptation and offers (partial) interpretability by identifying relevant attributes.
papers.limitation: Dependency on a pre-determined set of data attributes, which may not be comprehensive.
future_direction: Further investigation on the accordance of the derived attribute graph with domain priors.
Using only low-level and cheaply computable attributes.
Incorporating expert knowledge.
papers.abstract: Training generative models that capture rich semantics of the data and interpreting the latent representations encoded by such models are very important problems in un-/self-supervised learning. In this work, we provide a simple algorithm that relies on perturbation experiments on latent codes of a pre-trained generative autoencoder to uncover an attribute graph that is implied by the generative model. We perform perturbation experiments to check for influence of a given latent variable on a subset of attributes. Given this, we show that one can fit an effective graphical model that models a structural equation model between latent codes taken as exogenous variables and attributes taken as observed variables. One interesting aspect is that a single latent variable controls multiple overlapping subsets of attributes unlike conventional approaches that try to impose full independence. Using a pre-trained generative autoencoder trained on a large dataset of small molecules, we demonstrate that the graphical model between various molecular attributes and latent codes learned by our algorithm can be used to predict a specific property for molecules which are drawn from a different distribution. We compare prediction models trained on various feature subsets chosen by simple baselines, as well as existing causal discovery and sparse learning/feature selection methods, with the ones in the derived Markov blanket from our method. Results show empirically that the predictor that relies on our Markov blanket attributes is robust to distribution shifts when transferred or fine-tuned with a few samples from the new distribution, especially when training data is limited.

papers.title: Beyond performance: How design choices shape chemical language models
papers.research_question: How do design choices (molecular representation format, tokenization strategy, model architecture) influence the performance and chemical interpretability of chemical language models?
papers.core_contribution: Design choices, particularly molecular representation and tokenization, significantly affect the chemical interpretability of language models, with SMILES and atomwise tokenization yielding more chemically meaningful embeddings, even when downstream task performance is similar.
papers.conclusion: Design choices meaningfully shape how chemical information is represented in language models, and SMILES with atomwise tokenization is favorable for interpretability, guiding future development of chemically grounded CLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Atomwise tokenization generally yields better downstream performance than SentencePiece tokenization.
SMILES representations produce more chemically structured latent spaces than SELFIES representations.
BART and RoBERTa architectures yield comparably interpretable representations, but BART embeddings are more linearly separable for certain molecular properties.
RoBERTa shows a stronger ability to distinguish between atom types than BART.
The choice of molecular representation has a greater impact on interpretability than the model architecture.
future_direction: Exploring alternative molecular representations such as t-SMILES and DeepSMILES.
Comparing BART's generative capabilities with other large language model architectures like GPT.
Investigating the differences and synergies between large language models and graph-based approaches such as GROVER.
Utilizing highly curated datasets from specialized domains to reveal subtle chemical relationships.
papers.abstract: <title>Abstract</title> Chemical language models (CLMs) have shown strong performance in molecular property prediction and generation tasks. However, the impact of design choices, such as molecular representation format, tokenization strategy, and model architecture, on both performance and chemical interpretability remains underexplored. In this study, we systematically evaluate how these factors influence CLM performance and chemical understanding. We evaluated models through fine-tuning on downstream tasks and probing the structure of their latent spaces using simple classifiers and dimensionality reduction techniques.Despite similar performance on downstream tasks across model configurations, we observed substantial differences in the structure and interpretability of their internal representations. SMILES molecular representation format with atomwise tokenization strategy consistently produced more chemically meaningful embeddings, while models based on BART and RoBERTa architectures yielded comparably interpretable representations. These findings highlight that design choices meaningfully shape how chemical information is represented, even when external metrics appear unchanged. This insight can inform future model development, encouraging more chemically grounded and interpretable CLMs.

papers.title: NoiseCLR: A Contrastive Learning Approach for Unsupervised Discovery of Interpretable Directions in Diffusion Models
papers.research_question: How can we discover interpretable directions in the latent space of diffusion models in an unsupervised manner, without relying on text prompts or labeled data?
papers.core_contribution: We propose NoiseCLR, an unsupervised contrastive learning framework to discover interpretable directions in the latent space of text-to-image diffusion models without requiring text prompts, labeled data, or model fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: We present NoiseCLR, an unsupervised contrastive learning framework for discovering interpretable directions in diffusion models, enabling disentangled edits across multiple domains and competitive performance with state-of-the-art editing methods.
papers.key_findings:
NoiseCLR discovers diverse and fine-grained interpretable directions in diffusion models across multiple domains (faces, cats, cars, art) without supervision.
The learned directions are highly disentangled, allowing multiple edits within and across domains without interfering.
NoiseCLR outperforms existing diffusion-based and GAN-based editing methods in terms of disentanglement and edit quality, as shown by quantitative metrics and user studies.
The method requires only a small set of unlabeled images (around 100) per domain and does not require model fine-tuning.
Edits can be interpolated and applied to real images via DDIM inversion, providing control over the strength of the edit.
papers.limitation:
The method's capabilities are limited by the pre-trained Stable Diffusion model and CLIP, which may have biases and limitations.
Potential misuse for malicious purposes is a concern.
papers.abstract: Generative models have been very popular in the recent years for their image generation capabilities. GAN-based models are highly regarded for their disentangled latent space, which is a key feature contributing to their success in controlled image editing. On the other hand, diffusion models have emerged as powerful tools for generating high-quality images. However, the latent space of diffusion models is not as thoroughly explored or understood. Existing methods that aim to explore the latent space of diffusion models usually relies on text prompts to pinpoint specific semantics. However, this approach may be restrictive in areas such as art, fashion, or specialized fields like medicine, where suitable text prompts might not be available or easy to conceive thus limiting the scope of existing work. In this paper, we propose an unsupervised method to discover latent semantics in text-to-image diffusion models without relying on text prompts. Our method takes a small set of unlabeled images from specific domains, such as faces or cats, and a pre-trained diffusion model, and discovers diverse semantics in unsupervised fashion using a contrastive learning objective. Moreover, the learned directions can be applied simultaneously, either within the same domain (such as various types of facial edits) or across different domains (such as applying cat and face edits within the same image) without interfering with each other. Our extensive experiments show that our method achieves highly disentangled edits, outperforming existing approaches in both diffusion-based and GAN-based latent space editing methods.

papers.title: Interpreting GFlowNets for Drug Discovery: Extracting Actionable Insights for Medicinal Chemistry
papers.research_question: How can interpretability methods be adapted to structured generative models like GFlowNets to provide actionable insights for medicinal chemistry in drug discovery?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an interpretability framework for GFlowNets that reveals how SynFlowNet encodes chemical properties like polarity and lipophilicity, and provides actionable insights for drug discovery through counterfactual saliency and motif analysis.
papers.conclusion: The study extends interpretability tools to GFlowNets, showing that SynFlowNet's internal representations align with chemical intuition, and suggests future directions like multi-objective analysis and direct conditioning on physicochemical properties.
papers.key_findings:
Gradient-based saliency with counterfactual edits identifies atom- and motif-level regions that systematically affect predicted drug-likeness (QED).
Sparse autoencoders applied to SynFlowNet embeddings reveal latent factors that correlate strongly with physicochemical properties such as polarity, lipophilicity, and size.
Motif probes show that functional groups like halogens and aromatic rings are encoded in a linearly decodable manner in the embeddings.
The interpretability framework links model decisions to medicinal chemistry heuristics, enabling actionable insights for molecule design.
The approach demonstrates that GFlowNets can be interpreted using adapted methods from supervised learning, extending interpretability to structured generative policies.
papers.limitation:
Focuses primarily on QED, limiting generalization to multi-objective settings.
Disentanglement methods like sparse autoencoders and motif probes impose simple structure on the latent space, which may not capture complex reward landscapes.
Gradient-based saliency is only applied to the Stop action, missing intermediate decision points.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to multi-objective settings such as synthetic accessibility or binding affinity.
Condition GFlowNets directly on physicochemical properties for more interpretable representations.
Investigate the impact of interpretability tools on downstream molecule design and compare with alternative methods.
papers.abstract: Generative Flow Networks, or GFlowNets, offer a promising framework for molecular design, but their internal decision policies remain opaque. This limits adoption in drug discovery, where chemists require clear and interpretable rationales for proposed structures. We present an interpretability framework for SynFlowNet, a GFlowNet trained on documented chemical reactions and purchasable starting materials that generates both molecules and the synthetic routes that produce them. Our approach integrates three complementary components. Gradient based saliency combined with counterfactual perturbations identifies which atomic environments influence reward and how structural edits change molecular outcomes. Sparse autoencoders reveal axis aligned latent factors that correspond to physicochemical properties such as polarity, lipophilicity, and molecular size. Motif probes show that functional groups including aromatic rings and halogens are explicitly encoded and linearly decodable from the internal embeddings. Together, these results expose the chemical logic inside SynFlowNet and provide actionable and mechanistic insight that supports transparent and controllable molecular design.

papers.title: Superior Molecular Representations from Intermediate Encoder Layers
papers.research_question: Are we overlooking superior molecular representations by adhering to the final-layer convention in chemistry? Specifically, do intermediate layers of molecular encoders provide more informative and task-relevant features for downstream property prediction than the final layer?
papers.core_contribution: Intermediate layers of pretrained molecular encoders retain more general-purpose features and yield superior performance on downstream property prediction tasks compared to the final layer, both when used as frozen embeddings and when finetuned, leading to substantial performance improvements and computational efficiency.
papers.conclusion: The common practice of relying solely on final-layer representations from pretrained molecular encoders is suboptimal; exploring intermediate layers yields substantial performance gains and computational savings, advocating for a shift beyond the final-layer default.
papers.key_findings:
Using frozen embeddings from optimal intermediate layers improves downstream performance by an average of 5.4% (up to 28.6%) compared to the final-layer, with 81% of model-task combinations preferring a non-final layer.
Finetuning encoders truncated at intermediate depths achieves average improvements of 8.5% (up to 40.8%) over finetuning the complete encoder, with 71% of cases showing gains.
Label-free probes (tokenized-molecule entropy and adjacent-layer CKA) show that final layers undergo specialization and compression, while intermediate layers retain more transferable features.
The optimal intermediate layer varies by encoder architecture and downstream task; no single depth is universally best.
Frozen embedding performance correlates with finetuning performance (median Pearson correlation 0.60), providing an efficient proxy for selecting layers to finetune.
papers.limitation: The study is constrained by computational resources to five encoders and 22 ADMET tasks; extending the analysis to a broader set of molecular encoders and chemical domains could further validate the findings.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to a broader set of molecular encoders and chemical domains.
Conduct future work with additional architectures, multiple random seeds, and more exhaustive hyperparameter searches for deeper insights and more robust generalizations.
papers.abstract: Pretrained molecular encoders have become indispensable in computational chemistry for tasks such as property prediction and molecular generation. However, the standard practice of relying solely on final-layer embeddings for downstream tasks may discard valuable information. In this work, we first analyze the information flow in five diverse molecular encoders and find that intermediate layers retain more general-purpose features, whereas the final-layer specializes and compresses information. We then perform an empirical layer-wise evaluation across 22 property prediction tasks. We find that using frozen embeddings from optimal intermediate layers improves downstream performance by an average of 5.4%, up to 28.6%, compared to the final-layer. Furthermore, finetuning encoders truncated at intermediate depths achieves even greater average improvements of 8.5%, with increases as high as 40.8%, obtaining new state-of-the-art results on several benchmarks. These findings highlight the importance of exploring the full representational depth of molecular encoders to achieve substantial performance improvements and computational efficiency. The code will be made publicly available.

papers.title: Beyond the Black Box: Identifiable Interpretation and Control in Generative Models via Causal Minimality
papers.research_question: Under what theoretical conditions can we reliably identify meaningful, interpretable latent concepts within modern generative models? And what actionable, theoretically-grounded insights can advance both interpretability and controllability?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a theoretical framework based on causal minimality that provides conditions under which latent representations in generative models can be identified component-wise, enabling interpretable hierarchical concept graphs and fine-grained control.
papers.conclusion: The experiments illustrate the implications of the theorems and show how a principled, causal understanding can guide the application of established interpretation techniques.
papers.key_findings:
The principle of causal minimality, instantiated as sparsity constraints, enables the extraction of interpretable hierarchical concept graphs from text-to-image diffusion models.
The learned representations under these conditions are component-wise identifiable, meaning they correspond to true latent variables of the data-generating process.
These causally grounded concepts allow for fine-grained model steering, demonstrated in tasks like model unlearning, controllable generation, and multi-level editing.
papers.limitation: The theoretical assumptions, such as causal minimality and smoothness, may not hold universally in practice.
papers.abstract: Deep generative models, while revolutionizing fields like image and text generation, largely operate as opaque black boxes, hindering human understanding, control, and alignment. While methods like sparse autoencoders (SAEs) show remarkable empirical success, they often lack theoretical guarantees, risking subjective insights. Our primary objective is to establish a principled foundation for interpretable generative models. We demonstrate that the principle of causal minimality -- favoring the simplest causal explanation -- can endow the latent representations of diffusion vision and autoregressive language models with clear causal interpretation and robust, component-wise identifiable control. We introduce a novel theoretical framework for hierarchical selection models, where higher-level concepts emerge from the constrained composition of lower-level variables, better capturing the complex dependencies in data generation. Under theoretically derived minimality conditions (manifesting as sparsity or compression constraints), we show that learned representations can be equivalent to the true latent variables of the data-generating process. Empirically, applying these constraints to leading generative models allows us to extract their innate hierarchical concept graphs, offering fresh insights into their internal knowledge organization. Furthermore, these causally grounded concepts serve as levers for fine-grained model steering, paving the way for transparent, reliable systems.

papers.title: Dynamically Scaled Activation Steering
papers.research_question: How can activation steering be made adaptive so that interventions are applied only when necessary, decoupling when to steer from how to steer?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Dynamically Scaled Activation Steering (DSAS), a method-agnostic framework that adaptively modulates the strength of existing steering methods across layers and inputs, improving the trade-off between desired behavior (e.g., toxicity reduction) and model utility.
papers.conclusion: DSAS is an effective, general framework for conditional activation steering that decouples when to steer from how to steer, consistently improving the trade-off between behavior modification (e.g., toxicity mitigation) and model performance preservation across modalities.
papers.key_findings:
DSAS consistently improves the Pareto front for toxicity mitigation versus capability retention across different steering methods (CAA, ITI, LinEAS) and models (Qwen 2.5, Gemma 2).
DSAS can be trained end-to-end (E2E-DSAS) and matches or outperforms the vanilla DSAS.
DSAS works across modalities (text and image) without modification, enabling concept-specific modulation in text-to-image generation.
DSAS introduces minimal computational overhead and improves interpretability by pinpointing which tokens require steering and by how much.
DSAS outperforms recent conditional steering methods such as CAST and MERA in toxicity mitigation with higher performance retention.
papers.limitation: In image generation, the steering does not precisely localize the target concept spatially.
papers.abstract: Activation steering has emerged as a powerful method for guiding the behavior of generative models towards desired outcomes such as toxicity mitigation. However, most existing methods apply interventions uniformly across all inputs, degrading model performance when steering is unnecessary. We introduce Dynamically Scaled Activation Steering (DSAS), a method-agnostic steering framework that decouples when to steer from how to steer. DSAS adaptively modulates the strength of existing steering transformations across layers and inputs, intervening strongly only when undesired behavior is detected. At generation time, DSAS computes context-dependent scaling factors that selectively adjust the strength of any steering method. We also show how DSAS can be jointly optimized end-to-end together with the steering function. When combined with existing steering methods, DSAS consistently improves the Pareto front with respect to steering alone, achieving a better trade-off between toxicity mitigation and utility preservation. We further demonstrate DSAS's generality by applying it to a text-to-image diffusion model, showing how adaptive steering allows the modulation of specific concepts. Finally, DSAS introduces minimal computational overhead while improving interpretability, pinpointing which tokens require steering and by how much.

papers.title: Explainable Molecular Property Prediction: Aligning Chemical Concepts with Predictions via Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we provide chemically meaningful and faithful explanations for molecular property predictions using language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Lamole, a framework for explainable molecular property prediction that uses Group SELFIES representation and combines attention weights with gradients, calibrated by a marginal loss, to provide chemically meaningful and faithful explanations.
papers.conclusion: Lamole provides chemically meaningful and faithful explanations for molecular property prediction and can be integrated into an interpretable optimization pipeline for molecular design.
papers.key_findings:
Lamole achieves prediction accuracy comparable to state-of-the-art baselines while improving explanation accuracy by up to 14.3%.
The proposed information flow-based explanation method, integrating attention and gradients, captures interactions between functional groups.
The marginal loss aligns explanations with the tangent space of the data manifold, ensuring concept-aligned results.
Using only 10% of molecules with ground truth annotations can significantly improve explanation accuracy.
Integration with an evolutionary algorithm demonstrates Lamole's actionable utility for guiding molecular editing and optimization.
papers.limitation:
Complex interactions caused by multiple functional groups may not be fully captured, and other functional groups may receive relatively high importance scores.
The molecular editing case is a computational demonstration and does not imply real-world chemical optimality.
future_direction: Extending the framework to broader generalization scenarios, including unseen chemotypes.
Designing more strategies to reveal complex functional group interactions.
papers.abstract: Providing explainable molecular property predictions is critical for many scientific domains, such as drug discovery and material science. Though transformer-based language models have shown great potential in accurate molecular property prediction, they neither provide chemically meaningful explanations nor faithfully reveal the molecular structure-property relationships. In this work, we develop a framework for explainable molecular property prediction based on language models, dubbed as Lamole, which can provide chemical concepts-aligned explanations. We take a string-based molecular representation -- Group SELFIES -- as input tokens to pretrain and fine-tune our Lamole, as it provides chemically meaningful semantics. By disentangling the information flows of Lamole, we propose combining self-attention weights and gradients for better quantification of each chemically meaningful substructure's impact on the model's output. To make the explanations more faithfully respect the structure-property relationship, we then carefully craft a marginal loss to explicitly optimize the explanations to be able to align with the chemists' annotations. We bridge the manifold hypothesis with the elaborated marginal loss to prove that the loss can align the explanations with the tangent space of the data manifold, leading to concept-aligned explanations. Experimental results over six mutagenicity datasets and one hepatotoxicity dataset demonstrate Lamole can achieve comparable classification accuracy and boost the explanation accuracy by up to 14.3%, being the state-of-the-art in explainable molecular property prediction.

papers.title: EvolvED: Evolutionary Embeddings to Understand the Generation Process of Diffusion Models
papers.research_question: How can we holistically visualize and understand the iterative data evolution in diffusion models during generation?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces EvolvED, a method that provides a holistic visualization of the iterative generative process in diffusion models by combining tailored prompts, feature extraction, and a novel evolutionary embedding algorithm.
papers.conclusion: EvolvED provides a holistic view of the iterative generative process in diffusion models, enabling insights into data evolution and feature progression.
papers.key_findings:
EvolvED reveals how different object classes evolve at different rates during generation, with some (e.g., sharks, fruits) emerging earlier than others.
The method shows that context (e.g., background) is resolved before finer details in the generative process.
The evolutionary embedding preserves semantic neighborhoods while explicitly encoding iterations, enabling analysis of cluster evolution over time.
The radial layout optimizes space usage by allocating less area to early noisy iterations and more to later refined steps.
EvolvED is applicable to different diffusion models (GLIDE and Stable Diffusion) and can address various research questions about feature evolution.
papers.limitation:
The method relies on the choice of feature extractor, and mismatches between the extractor and prompt focus can lead to ineffective embeddings.
Early generation steps contain mostly noise, so there is a lack of structure, making analysis metrics less relevant for these steps.
papers.abstract: Diffusion models, widely used in image generation, rely on iterative refinement to generate images from noise. Understanding this data evolution is important for model development and interpretability, yet challenging due to its high-dimensional, iterative nature. Prior works often focus on static or instance-level analyses, missing the iterative and holistic aspects of the generative path. While dimensionality reduction can visualize image evolution for few instances, it does preserve the iterative structure. To address these gaps, we introduce EvolvED, a method that presents a holistic view of the iterative generative process in diffusion models. EvolvED goes beyond instance exploration by leveraging predefined research questions to streamline generative space exploration. Tailored prompts aligned with these questions are used to extract intermediate images, preserving iterative context. Targeted feature extractors trace the evolution of key image attribute evolution, addressing the complexity of high-dimensional outputs. Central to EvolvED is a novel evolutionary embedding algorithm that encodes iterative steps while maintaining semantic relations. It enhances the visualization of data evolution by clustering semantically similar elements within each iteration with t-SNE, grouping elements by iteration, and aligning an instance's elements across iterations. We present rectilinear and radial layouts to represent iterations and support exploration. We apply EvolvED to diffusion models like GLIDE and Stable Diffusion, demonstrating its ability to provide valuable insights into the generative process.

papers.title: Emergence and Evolution of Interpretable Concepts in Diffusion Models
papers.research_question: What level of image representation is present in the early stage of the generative process? How do visual representations evolve through various stages? Can the uncovered concepts be used to steer the generative process interpretably, and how does intervention effectiveness depend on diffusion time?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uses Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to uncover interpretable concepts in diffusion model activations, showing that image composition emerges very early in the diffusion process. It introduces intervention techniques that can control composition in early stages and style in middle stages.
papers.conclusion: The semantic layout of the image emerges as early as the first reverse diffusion step and can be predicted from SAE features. Intervention experiments show that SAE features can control image composition in early stages and image style in middle stages.
papers.key_findings:
Image composition emerges as early as the first reverse diffusion step, even though the model output contains no visual clues.
Image composition is finalized by the middle of the reverse diffusion process.
Spatially targeted interventions can control image composition in early stages but not in later stages.
Global interventions can control image style in middle stages but not in early or final stages.
Concepts become more refined and distinct as generation progresses (increased concept cohesion and separability).
papers.limitation: Leakage effect rooted in the U-Net architecture, which enables information to bypass interventions through skip connections.
future_direction: Developing editing techniques that adapt to the evolving nature of diffusion representations.
Extending the work to diffusion transformers to tackle the leakage challenge.
papers.abstract: Diffusion models have become the go-to method for text-to-image generation, producing high-quality images from pure noise. However, the inner workings of diffusion models is still largely a mystery due to their black-box nature and complex, multi-step generation process. Mechanistic interpretability techniques, such as Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs), have been successful in understanding and steering the behavior of large language models at scale. However, the great potential of SAEs has not yet been applied toward gaining insight into the intricate generative process of diffusion models. In this work, we leverage the SAE framework to probe the inner workings of a popular text-to-image diffusion model, and uncover a variety of human-interpretable concepts in its activations. Interestingly, we find that even before the first reverse diffusion step is completed, the final composition of the scene can be predicted surprisingly well by looking at the spatial distribution of activated concepts. Moreover, going beyond correlational analysis, we design intervention techniques aimed at manipulating image composition and style, and demonstrate that (1) in early stages of diffusion image composition can be effectively controlled, (2) in the middle stages image composition is finalized, however stylistic interventions are effective, and (3) in the final stages only minor textural details are subject to change.

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability of Diffusion Models: Circuit-Level Analysis and Causal Validation
papers.research_question: How do diffusion models internally process and transform information during the denoising procedure, and what are the computational circuits and mechanisms underlying image generation?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a quantitative circuit-level analysis framework for diffusion models, revealing systematic algorithmic differences in how they process synthetic versus naturalistic data, identifying specialized attention mechanisms, and providing causal validation through intervention experiments.
papers.conclusion: This work establishes the first comprehensive circuit-level analysis of diffusion models, providing quantitative foundations for mechanistic interpretability and revealing systematic algorithmic differences between synthetic and naturalistic data processing with implications for model control and architecture design.
papers.key_findings:
Real-world face processing requires circuits with measurably higher computational complexity than synthetic data processing, though with variability across model initializations.
Eight functionally distinct attention mechanisms with specialized computational roles (e.g., edge detection, texture analysis, semantic understanding) were identified and quantified.
Temporal activation analysis reveals distinct processing phases across the denoising process, with some attention heads specializing in early structure formation and others in detail refinement.
Intervention analysis identifies critical computational bottlenecks, with targeted ablations producing performance degradation from 25.6% to 153.8%.
Circuit transferability varies with abstraction level and temporal phase, suggesting a hierarchical organization of fundamental and domain-specific computations.
papers.limitation:
The analysis focuses on facial image generation using synthetic and CelebA datasets, which may limit generalizability to other image domains.
The model used is a 262M parameter architecture, substantially smaller than state-of-the-art diffusion models, which may limit the discovery of emergent capabilities and circuit complexity present in larger models.
While intervention analysis provides evidence for circuit functionality, more sophisticated causal analysis methods could strengthen mechanistic claims.
The correlation between attention head entropy and peak activation timing did not reach statistical significance, suggesting head specialization is multidimensional.
future_direction: Extending the circuit analysis methodologies to larger-scale diffusion models and diverse generation tasks.
Developing more sophisticated causal analysis techniques for understanding generative model computation.
Extending the methodologies to text-to-image generation and other cross-modal tasks.
papers.abstract: We present a quantitative circuit-level analysis of diffusion models, establishing computational pathways and mechanistic principles underlying image generation processes. Through systematic intervention experiments across 2,000 synthetic and 2,000 CelebA facial images, we discover fundamental algorithmic differences in how diffusion architectures process synthetic versus naturalistic data distributions. Our investigation reveals that real-world face processing requires circuits with measurably higher computational complexity (complexity ratio = 1.084 plus/minus 0.008, p < 0.001), exhibiting distinct attention specialization patterns with entropy divergence ranging from 0.015 to 0.166 across denoising timesteps. We identify eight functionally distinct attention mechanisms showing specialized computational roles: edge detection (entropy = 3.18 plus/minus 0.12), texture analysis (entropy = 4.16 plus/minus 0.08), and semantic understanding (entropy = 2.67 plus/minus 0.15). Intervention analysis demonstrates critical computational bottlenecks where targeted ablations produce 25.6% to 128.3% performance degradation, providing causal evidence for identified circuit functions. These findings establish quantitative foundations for algorithmic understanding and control of generative model behavior through mechanistic intervention strategies.

papers.title: Unsupervised Discovery of Semantic Latent Directions in Diffusion Models
papers.research_question: How can we discover semantic latent directions in the latent space of diffusion models in an unsupervised manner to enable controllable image editing?
papers.core_contribution: An unsupervised method to discover semantic latent directions in diffusion models using Riemannian geometry and the pullback metric, enabling controllable image editing without external supervision.
papers.conclusion: The proposed unsupervised approach successfully discovers semantic latent directions in diffusion models, providing insights into the geometry of the latent space and enabling semantic image editing without external supervision.
papers.key_findings:
Semantic latent directions found in an unsupervised manner lead to mostly disentangled attribute changes in generated images.
Editing in earlier timesteps (closer to T) changes coarse attributes, while editing in later timesteps focuses on high-frequency details.
The latent space X is a curved manifold, and spherical linear interpolation (slerp) is approximately geodesic, leading to smoother interpolations.
Global semantic directions can be found by averaging local directions and are consistent across different samples.
The method generalizes to Stable Diffusion, showing similar coarse-to-fine editing behavior in its learned latent space.
papers.limitation:
Entanglement between attributes due to dataset prior, e.g., the direction for long hair also converts male subjects to female.
Abrupt changes during editing in Stable Diffusion, possibly due to a more complex manifold or the influence of conditional guidance.
future_direction: Analyzing latent directions in conditions such as text prompts or segmentation labels.
papers.abstract: Despite the success of diffusion models (DMs), we still lack a thorough understanding of their latent space. While image editing with GANs builds upon latent space, DMs rely on editing the conditions such as text prompts. We present an unsupervised method to discover interpretable editing directions for the latent variables $\mathbf{x}_t \in \mathcal{X}$ of DMs. Our method adopts Riemannian geometry between $\mathcal{X}$ and the intermediate feature maps $\mathcal{H}$ of the U-Nets to provide a deep understanding over the geometrical structure of $\mathcal{X}$. The discovered semantic latent directions mostly yield disentangled attribute changes, and they are globally consistent across different samples. Furthermore, editing in earlier timesteps edits coarse attributes, while ones in later timesteps focus on high-frequency details. We define the curvedness of a line segment between samples to show that $\mathcal{X}$ is a curved manifold. Experiments on different baselines and datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our method even on Stable Diffusion. Our source code will be publicly available for the future researchers.

papers.title: Trade-offs in Fine-tuned Diffusion Models Between Accuracy and Interpretability
papers.research_question: What is the trade-off between image fidelity (accuracy) and interpretability in fine-tuned diffusion models, particularly when fine-tuning with a learnable versus frozen text encoder?
papers.core_contribution: Fine-tuning diffusion models with a frozen text encoder preserves interpretability (measured via attention map localization) at a slight cost to image quality, whereas fine-tuning with a learnable text encoder improves image quality but severely degrades interpretability.
papers.conclusion: There is a trade-off between accuracy and interpretability in fine-tuned diffusion models; freezing the language encoder during fine-tuning preserves interpretability while maintaining reasonable generative performance, which is crucial for applications like medical imaging.
papers.key_findings:
Fine-tuning with a learnable text encoder (Finetune L) yields better image quality (lower FID) but poor interpretability (low localization metrics).
Fine-tuning with a frozen text encoder (Finetune F) retains high interpretability (good localization) with only a modest decrease in image quality.
The frozen encoder method (Finetune F) outperforms discriminative phrase grounding methods on two out of eight disease classes in a zero-shot manner.
The variability of text input affects interpretability: higher variability (e.g., full radiology impressions) leads to better interpretability than low-variability prompts (e.g., single class labels).
In models with learnable text encoders, the end-of-string token often shows high localization performance, but this is not reliable for phrase grounding as it does not associate specific words with image regions.
papers.limitation:
FID has limitations as a generative quality metric because it is a trained metric and requires many samples to be accurate.
Conditional generation evaluation is limited by the lack of ground-truth data for generated images.
future_direction: Large-scale study with domain experts to evaluate which metric (e.g., FID vs. CNR) better captures generative quality in relation to human judgment.
Design of interpretable generative models for medical applications by considering the trade-off between fidelity and interpretability.
papers.abstract: Recent advancements in diffusion models have significantly impacted the trajectory of generative machine learning research, with many adopting the strategy of fine-tuning pre-trained models using domain-specific text-to-image datasets. Notably, this method has been readily employed for medical applications, such as X-ray image synthesis, leveraging the plethora of associated radiology reports. Yet, a prevailing concern is the lack of assurance on whether these models genuinely comprehend their generated content. With the evolution of text-conditional image generation, these models have grown potent enough to facilitate object localization scrutiny. Our research underscores this advancement in the critical realm of medical imaging, emphasizing the crucial role of interpretability. We further unravel a consequential trade-off between image fidelity as gauged by conventional metrics and model interpretability in generative diffusion models. Specifically, the adoption of learnable text encoders when fine-tuning results in diminished interpretability. Our in-depth exploration uncovers the underlying factors responsible for this divergence. Consequently, we present a set of design principles for the development of truly interpretable generative models. Code is available at https://github.com/MischaD/chest-distillation.

papers.title: InterPLM: Discovering Interpretable Features in Protein Language Models via Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: What do protein language models (PLMs) learn internally, and how can we extract and analyze interpretable features from their representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a systematic framework using sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to extract and analyze interpretable features from protein language models, revealing features that correlate with known biological concepts and enabling applications like filling missing annotations and steering sequence generation.
papers.conclusion: Protein language models encode rich, interpretable representations of protein biology, and the SAE-based framework successfully extracts these features, recovering both known biology and potentially new protein motifs.
papers.key_findings:
SAE features capture significantly more biological annotations (up to 2,548 features per layer) than individual neurons in ESM-2 (up to 46 per layer).
Features cluster based on shared functional and structural roles, revealing hierarchical relationships and subtle specializations.
Large language models (Claude-3.5 Sonnet) can generate meaningful descriptions of SAE features, with high correlation between predicted and actual activation patterns.
Feature activation patterns can identify missing annotations in protein databases and suggest novel biological motifs.
Targeted steering of specific feature activations can influence the model's sequence predictions in interpretable ways.
papers.limitation:
Scaling this approach to structure-prediction models like ESMFold or AlphaFold is a crucial next step.
Steering experiments are currently limited to simple contexts (e.g., periodic glycine patterns); extending steering to more complex biological concepts remains challenging.
The analysis focuses only on representations of unmasked amino acids, leaving open questions about masked token embeddings and the CLS token.
future_direction: Scaling the approach to structure-prediction models like ESMFold or AlphaFold.
Improving feature interpretability through advances in SAE training and additional evaluation metrics.
Mapping how features combine into interpretable circuits for specific capabilities like 3D contact prediction.
papers.abstract: Protein language models (PLMs) have demonstrated remarkable success in protein modeling and design, yet their internal mechanisms for predicting structure and function remain poorly understood. Here we present a systematic approach to extract and analyze interpretable features from PLMs using sparse autoencoders (SAEs). By training SAEs on embeddings from the PLM ESM-2, we identify up to 2,548 human-interpretable latent features per layer that strongly correlate with up to 143 known biological concepts such as binding sites, structural motifs, and functional domains. In contrast, examining individual neurons in ESM-2 reveals up to 46 neurons per layer with clear conceptual alignment across 15 known concepts, suggesting that PLMs represent most concepts in superposition. Beyond capturing known annotations, we show that ESM-2 learns coherent concepts that do not map onto existing annotations and propose a pipeline using language models to automatically interpret novel latent features learned by the SAEs. As practical applications, we demonstrate how these latent features can fill in missing annotations in protein databases and enable targeted steering of protein sequence generation. Our results demonstrate that PLMs encode rich, interpretable representations of protein biology and we propose a systematic framework to extract and analyze these latent features. In the process, we recover both known biology and potentially new protein motifs. As community resources, we introduce InterPLM (interPLM.ai), an interactive visualization platform for exploring and analyzing learned PLM features, and release code for training and analysis at github.com/ElanaPearl/interPLM.

papers.title: Causal Intervention Framework for Variational Auto Encoder Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: The paper investigates how Causal Effect Strength (CES) relates to traditional disentanglement metrics across VAE architectures, the effectiveness of disentanglement penalties based on factor count and latent dimensionality, whether causal metrics can reveal mechanistic differences not captured by traditional metrics, and how continuous interventions behave on discrete latent representations.
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces the first multi-level causal intervention framework for mechanistic interpretability of VAEs, with new metrics (CES, specificity, modularity), and empirically reveals key findings like the CES-DCI trade-off and β-VAE capacity bottleneck.
papers.conclusion: The framework and metrics advance mechanistic understanding of VAEs, revealing fundamental trade-offs and dataset-dependent optimality, with implications for model design and evaluation.
papers.key_findings:
A consistent within-dataset negative correlation between Causal Effect Strength (CES) and DCI disentanglement, termed the CES-DCI trade-off.
The KL reweighting mechanism of β-VAE causes a capacity bottleneck when generative factors approach latent dimensionality, degrading disentanglement on complex datasets.
No single VAE architecture is best across all datasets; optimal choice depends on dataset structure.
Continuous intervention metrics like CES yield near-zero values for discrete latent spaces (VQ-VAE), highlighting a limitation.
Causal intervention metrics provide mechanistic insights not captured by traditional disentanglement metrics.
papers.limitation:
DCI metric numerical instability due to dead latent dimensions producing infinite values.
FactorVAE hyperparameter interaction with batch size may underestimate disentanglement ability.
Training duration of 30 epochs may not ensure full convergence for all models.
Fixed latent dimensionality of 10 may affect capacity bottleneck conclusions.
CES metric combines magnitude and spatial extent, lacking finer decomposition.
future_direction: Extending the framework to other generative architectures like diffusion models and normalizing flows.
Developing discrete-native interpretability tools for quantized generative models.
Investigating how latent dimensionality interacts with disentanglement penalties.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability of deep learning models has emerged as a crucial research direction for understanding the functioning of neural networks. While significant progress has been made in interpreting discriminative models like transformers, understanding generative models such as Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) remains challenging. This paper introduces a comprehensive causal intervention framework for mechanistic interpretability of VAEs. We develop techniques to identify and analyze "circuit motifs" in VAEs, examining how semantic factors are encoded, processed, and disentangled through the network layers. Our approach uses targeted interventions at different levels: input manipulations, latent space perturbations, activation patching, and causal mediation analysis. We apply our framework to both synthetic datasets with known causal relationships and standard disentanglement benchmarks. Results show that our interventions can successfully isolate functional circuits, map computational graphs to causal graphs of semantic factors, and distinguish between polysemantic and monosemantic units. Furthermore, we introduce metrics for causal effect strength, intervention specificity, and circuit modularity that quantify the interpretability of VAE components. Experimental results demonstrate clear differences between VAE variants, with FactorVAE achieving higher disentanglement scores (0.084) and effect strengths (mean 4.59) compared to standard VAE (0.064, 3.99) and Beta-VAE (0.051, 3.43). Our framework advances the mechanistic understanding of generative models and provides tools for more transparent and controllable VAE architectures.

papers.title: MolEdit: Knowledge Editing for Multimodal Molecule Language Models
papers.research_question: How to edit knowledge in multimodal molecule language models (MoLMs) to correct inaccuracies while preserving unrelated knowledge, specifically for molecule-to-caption and caption-to-molecule generation tasks.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces MolEdit, a framework for editing multimodal molecule language models, and MEBench, a benchmark for evaluating such editing, addressing molecule-specific challenges of multifaceted expertise and cross-molecule interdependence.
papers.conclusion: MolEdit provides an effective framework for editing multimodal molecule language models, enabling precise knowledge updates while preserving unrelated information, and MEBench offers a comprehensive evaluation benchmark, charting a path toward safer, continuously updatable scientific foundation models.
papers.key_findings:
MolEdit outperforms fine-tuning, gradient-based (MEND), and memory-based (GRACE) baselines across Reliability, Locality, and Generality metrics on both MoMu and MolFM backbones.
MolEdit achieves up to 18.8% higher Reliability and 12.0% better Locality than state-of-the-art editing baselines.
Editing molecule generation is more challenging than editing caption generation, and performance is generally better on MoMu than on MolFM.
The Multi-Expert Knowledge Adapter (MEKA) effectively routes different facets of molecular knowledge to specialized experts, and the Expertise-Aware Editing Switcher (EAES) accurately activates edits only for relevant inputs.
Ablation studies confirm the contribution of each component (MEKA and EAES) to MolEdit's overall performance.
papers.limitation:
Editing molecular SMILES strings is inherently more complex and abstract than editing captions, lacking explicit semantic structure.
Potential misuse of editing to amplify unsafe molecular knowledge and inadvertent propagation of dataset biases.
future_direction: Future work on editing MoLMs.
papers.abstract: Understanding and continuously refining multimodal molecular knowledge is crucial for advancing biomedicine, chemistry, and materials science. Molecule language models (MoLMs) have become powerful tools in these domains, integrating structural representations (e.g., SMILES strings, molecular graphs) with rich contextual descriptions (e.g., physicochemical properties). However, MoLMs can encode and propagate inaccuracies due to outdated web-mined training corpora or malicious manipulation, jeopardizing downstream discovery pipelines. While knowledge editing has been explored for general-domain AI, its application to MoLMs remains uncharted, presenting unique challenges due to the multifaceted and interdependent nature of molecular knowledge. In this paper, we take the first step toward MoLM editing for two critical tasks: molecule-to-caption generation and caption-to-molecule generation. To address molecule-specific challenges, we propose MolEdit, a powerful framework that enables targeted modifications while preserving unrelated molecular knowledge. MolEdit combines a Multi-Expert Knowledge Adapter that routes edits to specialized experts for different molecular facets with an Expertise-Aware Editing Switcher that activates the adapters only when input closely matches the stored edits across all expertise, minimizing interference with unrelated knowledge. To systematically evaluate editing performance, we introduce MEBench, a comprehensive benchmark assessing multiple dimensions, including Reliability (accuracy of the editing), Locality (preservation of irrelevant knowledge), and Generality (robustness to reformed queries). Across extensive experiments on two popular MoLM backbones, MolEdit delivers up to 18.8% higher Reliability and 12.0% better Locality than baselines while maintaining efficiency. The code is available at: https://github.com/LzyFischer/MolEdit.

papers.title: ExpertSteer: Intervening in LLMs through Expert Knowledge
papers.research_question: How can we guide LLMs to follow desired behaviors during inference by leveraging external expert models for activation steering, overcoming limitations of existing methods that rely on the model itself?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes EXPERTSTEER, a method that leverages external expert models to generate steering vectors for activation steering in LLMs, enabling effective knowledge transfer without updating model parameters.
papers.conclusion: EXPERTSTEER is an effective and efficient activation steering method that enables knowledge transfer from any expert model to arbitrary target LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
EXPERTSTEER outperforms existing activation steering methods across diverse tasks and models.
It works effectively in both same-family and cross-family model settings.
RFMs are more effective for feature extraction compared to linear methods like PCA and mean difference.
The choice of expert model is crucial for effective steering.
EXPERTSTEER is computationally efficient.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable capabilities across various tasks, yet guiding them to follow desired behaviours during inference remains a significant challenge. Activation steering offers a promising method to control the generation process of LLMs by modifying their internal activations. However, existing methods commonly intervene in the model's behaviour using steering vectors generated by the model itself, which constrains their effectiveness to that specific model and excludes the possibility of leveraging powerful external expert models for steering. To address these limitations, we propose ExpertSteer, a novel approach that leverages arbitrary specialized expert models to generate steering vectors, enabling intervention in any LLMs. ExpertSteer transfers the knowledge from an expert model to a target LLM through a cohesive four-step process: first aligning representation dimensions with auto-encoders to enable cross-model transfer, then identifying intervention layer pairs based on mutual information analysis, next generating steering vectors from the expert model using Recursive Feature Machines, and finally applying these vectors on the identified layers during inference to selectively guide the target LLM without updating model parameters. We conduct comprehensive experiments using three LLMs on 15 popular benchmarks across four distinct domains. Experiments demonstrate that ExpertSteer significantly outperforms established baselines across diverse tasks at minimal cost.

papers.title: Explainability Techniques for Chemical Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we explain the predictions of chemical language models by attributing importance to individual atoms in the input molecular string?
papers.core_contribution: We propose an explainable AI technique for chemical language models that attributes the importance of individual atoms to the model's predictions by backpropagating relevance through attention scores and gradients, and visualize the importance on the molecular structure.
papers.conclusion: We propose an attribution technique for Transformers operating on molecular string representations, which provides interpretable predictions and allows inspection of the model's learned features for solubility prediction.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed method achieves competitive predictive performance on aqueous and organic solvent solubility prediction tasks.
The visualizations highlight atoms that are important for solubility, which can be validated by chemists.
The model sometimes attributes high relevance to the carbon backbone, which may be due to the pretraining procedure.
The method is applicable to self-attention Transformers and can be extended to other architectures.
papers.limitation:
The method only visualizes atom tokens and does not handle non-atom tokens (e.g., bonds, brackets) in the SMILES string.
The model does not enforce invariance to different SMILES representations of the same molecule.
future_direction: Extend the visualization to non-atom tokens in the SMILES string.
Enforce SMILES invariance in the model through contrastive training.
Apply the explainability technique to other Transformer architectures, such as generative models.
papers.abstract: Explainability techniques are crucial in gaining insights into the reasons behind the predictions of deep learning models, which have not yet been applied to chemical language models. We propose an explainable AI technique that attributes the importance of individual atoms towards the predictions made by these models. Our method backpropagates the relevance information towards the chemical input string and visualizes the importance of individual atoms. We focus on self-attention Transformers operating on molecular string representations and leverage a pretrained encoder for finetuning. We showcase the method by predicting and visualizing solubility in water and organic solvents. We achieve competitive model performance while obtaining interpretable predictions, which we use to inspect the pretrained model.

papers.title: Revealing Token-Level Importance in Conditional Molecular Design Through Kullback–Leibler Divergence
papers.research_question: How can we explain conditional molecular design models by quantifying the influence of property conditions on the generative process to reveal token-level importance?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a method to interpret conditional molecular design models using Kullback-Leibler Divergence to quantify the token-level importance of property conditions during generation.
papers.conclusion: Introduced a novel method for interpreting conditional molecular design models using KL divergence to quantify the influence of property conditions.
future_direction: Analyze how perturbations on the most important tokens affect predicted property values
Compare the explainability method with other approaches in the literature
Assess generalization to other textual- and graph-based molecular representations
papers.abstract: Conditional molecular design using transformer-based models can accelerate drug discovery, but their black-box nature limits interpretability. We propose a method to explain these models by quantifying the influence of property conditions on the generative process. Our approach uses the Kullback–Leibler Divergence to measure the difference between conditional and unconditional output distributions at each generation step. This allows us to identify the token-level importance of a sequence for specific desired conditions.

papers.title: Exploring the Representation Manifolds of Stable Diffusion Through the Lens of Intrinsic Dimension
papers.research_question: How do prompts affect the intrinsic dimension of internal representations in Stable Diffusion?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that prompt choice significantly affects the intrinsic dimension of representations in Stable Diffusion, with correlation to prompt perplexity in bottleneck layers.
papers.conclusion: Intrinsic dimension could be a useful tool for future studies of the impact of different prompts on text-to-image models.
papers.key_findings:
Prompts have a substantial effect on the intrinsic dimension of internal representations, with variations up to 10 dimensions.
Intrinsic dimension in latent representations decreases monotonically during denoising, while in bottleneck representations it forms a U-shaped curve.
In bottleneck layers, intrinsic dimension correlates with prompt perplexity, suggesting that less likely prompts result in higher-dimensional representations.
The dynamics of intrinsic dimension over denoising steps depend on the layer from which representations are extracted.
The time step embedding vector contributes to the increase in intrinsic dimension in bottleneck representations at later denoising steps.
papers.limitation: The correlation between perplexity and intrinsic dimension must be treated with caution, as it is not observed in latent representations.
future_direction: Adapting the experiments to other text-to-image models like DALL-E.
Comparing perplexity scores with actual frequencies of prompt tokens in training data like LAION-5B.
More comprehensive studies of other models that utilize prompts.
papers.abstract: Prompting has become an important mechanism by which users can more effectively interact with many flavors of foundation model. Indeed, the last several years have shown that well-honed prompts can sometimes unlock emergent capabilities within such models. While there has been a substantial amount of empirical exploration of prompting within the community, relatively few works have studied prompting at a mathematical level. In this work we aim to take a first step towards understanding basic geometric properties induced by prompts in Stable Diffusion, focusing on the intrinsic dimension of internal representations within the model. We find that choice of prompt has a substantial impact on the intrinsic dimension of representations at both layers of the model which we explored, but that the nature of this impact depends on the layer being considered. For example, in certain bottleneck layers of the model, intrinsic dimension of representations is correlated with prompt perplexity (measured using a surrogate model), while this correlation is not apparent in the latent layers. Our evidence suggests that intrinsic dimension could be a useful tool for future studies of the impact of different prompts on text-to-image models.

papers.title: Interpretable Diffusion Models with B-cos Networks
papers.research_question: How can text-to-image diffusion models be made inherently interpretable to provide insight into how individual prompt tokens affect the generated image?
papers.core_contribution: This paper integrates B-cos networks into text-to-image diffusion models, providing inherent interpretability and token-level attributions that link output pixels to prompt tokens, enabling the detection of missing concepts in generated images.
papers.conclusion: B-cos networks can be effectively used in text-to-image diffusion models to provide inherent interpretability, with explanations that faithfully capture the alignment between an image and its prompt, enabling the detection of missing concepts.
papers.key_findings:
B-cos networks can be effectively integrated into diffusion models, providing faithful explanations of prompt-image alignment.
The proposed method yields token-level attributions that consistently assign higher relevance scores to semantically meaningful tokens.
The explanations can identify failure cases where the generated image does not align with the prompt, such as a missing object.
The model summary (dynamic linear transformation) effectively captures the underlying computations, as shown by the close match between normalized reconstructions and model outputs.
Using deterministic sampling (DDIM with σ=0) avoids introducing biases that would break the completeness of the B-cos summary.
papers.limitation: The approach currently leads to reduced generative performance (lower image quality) compared to standard diffusion models.
future_direction: Developing methods to overcome the trade-off between interpretability and generative performance.
papers.abstract: Text-to-image diffusion models generate images by iteratively denoising random noise, conditioned on a prompt. While these models have enabled impressive progress in image generation, they often fail to accurately reflect all semantic information described in the prompt -- failures that are difficult to detect automatically. In this work, we introduce a diffusion model architecture built with B-cos modules that offers inherent interpretability. Our approach provides insight into how individual prompt tokens affect the generated image by producing explanations that highlight the pixel regions influenced by each token. We demonstrate that B-cos diffusion models can produce high-quality images while providing meaningful insights into prompt-image alignment.

papers.title: Partnering with Radical AI to Advance Materials Science With Interpretability
