papers.abstract: In deep learning for drug discovery, chemical data are often represented as simplified molecular-input line-entry system (SMILES) sequences which allow for straightforward implementation of natural language processing methodologies, one being the sequence-to-sequence autoencoder. However, we observe that training an autoencoder solely on SMILES is insufficient to learn molecular representations that are semantically meaningful, where semantics are defined by the structural (graph-to-graph) similarities between molecules. We demonstrate by example that autoencoders may map structurally similar molecules to distant codes, resulting in an incoherent latent space that does not respect the structural similarities between molecules. To address this shortcoming we propose Semantically-Aware Latent Space Autoencoder (SALSA), a transformer-autoencoder modified with a contrastive task, tailored specifically to learn graph-to-graph similarity between molecules. Formally, the contrastive objective is to map structurally similar molecules (separated by a single graph edit) to nearby codes in the latent space. To accomplish this, we generate a novel dataset comprised of sets of structurally similar molecules and opt for a supervised contrastive loss that is able to incorporate full sets of positive samples. We compare SALSA to its ablated counterparts, and show empirically that the composed training objective (reconstruction and contrastive task) leads to a higher quality latent space that is more 1) structurally-aware, 2) semantically continuous, and 3) property-aware.

papers.title: Diffusion Models Generate Images Like Painters: an Analytical Theory of Outline First, Details Later
papers.research_question: How do diffusion generative models convert pure noise into meaningful images? The paper investigates whether diffusion models generate images by first committing to an outline and then adding details, and provides a theoretical explanation for this behavior.
papers.core_contribution: The paper derives a closed-form solution to the probability flow ODE for a Gaussian distribution, which explains the 'outline-first, details-later' behavior in diffusion models and can be used to accelerate sampling by skipping early steps.
papers.conclusion: Diffusion models generate images by first committing to an outline and then adding finer details, similar to how painters work. The theoretical analysis provides a geometric understanding of the diffusion process and links it to image retrieval.
papers.key_findings:
Reverse diffusion trajectories are effectively two-dimensional and resemble rotations within the plane defined by the initial noise and final image.
High-variance scene features (e.g., layout) emerge earlier in the generation process than low-variance details.
Early perturbations during reverse diffusion have a greater impact on image content than later perturbations.
The Gaussian solution accurately predicts the early phase of reverse diffusion for pre-trained models.
A hybrid sampling method that uses the Gaussian solution to skip early steps can accelerate generation without degrading image quality.
papers.limitation:
The Gaussian approximation is only accurate early in reverse diffusion and breaks down later when the distribution becomes multi-modal.
For larger images, the Gaussian approximation is less effective due to difficulties in estimating the covariance matrix from limited data.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to other diffusion formulations such as Poisson flow generative models.
Combine the acceleration method with other advanced samplers.
papers.abstract: How do diffusion generative models convert pure noise into meaningful images? In a variety of pretrained diffusion models (including conditional latent space models like Stable Diffusion), we observe that the reverse diffusion process that underlies image generation has the following properties: (i) individual trajectories tend to be low-dimensional and resemble 2D `rotations'; (ii) high-variance scene features like layout tend to emerge earlier, while low-variance details tend to emerge later; and (iii) early perturbations tend to have a greater impact on image content than later perturbations. To understand these phenomena, we derive and study a closed-form solution to the probability flow ODE for a Gaussian distribution, which shows that the reverse diffusion state rotates towards a gradually-specified target on the image manifold. It also shows that generation involves first committing to an outline, and then to finer and finer details. We find that this solution accurately describes the initial phase of image generation for pretrained models, and can in principle be used to make image generation more efficient by skipping reverse diffusion steps. Finally, we use our solution to characterize the image manifold in Stable Diffusion. Our viewpoint reveals an unexpected similarity between generation by GANs and diffusion and provides a conceptual link between diffusion and image retrieval.

papers.title: Peering inside the black box: Learning the relevance of many-body functions in Neural Network potentials
papers.research_question: How can machine learned coarse-grained potentials based on graph neural networks be interpreted in terms of physically meaningful many-body contributions to the total energy?
papers.core_contribution: Extends GNN-LRP to interpret coarse-grained neural network potentials, showing the learned energy can be decomposed into physically meaningful many-body contributions.
papers.conclusion: GNN-LRP provides a way to interpret machine learned coarse-grained potentials, showing the learned interactions are physically meaningful and offering insights into molecular systems.
papers.key_findings:
For methane and water, 2-body relevance scores show repulsive interactions at short distances and, for water, stabilizing interactions at the first solvation shell.
3-body interactions are crucial for water to recover structural properties, with relevance scores indicating stabilizing and destabilizing contributions.
For protein NTL9, relevance scores identify stabilizing interactions in the folded state and can distinguish between two folding pathways.
The method can analyze the effect of mutations by changing bead embeddings, showing the model learns amino-acid specific interactions.
Different GNN architectures (PaiNN and SO3Net) learn similar underlying physical interactions despite different functional representations.
future_direction: Refining the concepts to provide greater insight and systematic choice of architecture and functionalization.
papers.abstract: Machine learned potentials are becoming a popular tool to define an effective energy model for complex systems, either incorporating electronic structure effects at the atomistic resolution, or effectively renormalizing part of the atomistic degrees of freedom at a coarse-grained resolution. One of the main criticisms to machine learned potentials is that the energy inferred by the network is not as interpretable as in more traditional approaches where a simpler functional form is used. Here we address this problem by extending tools recently proposed in the nascent field of Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) to coarse-grained potentials based on graph neural networks (GNN). We demonstrate the approach on three different coarse-grained systems including two fluids (methane and water) and the protein NTL9. On these examples, we show that the neural network potentials can be in practice decomposed in relevance contributions to different orders, that can be directly interpreted and provide physical insights on the systems of interest.

papers.title: From Neurons to Neutrons: A Case Study in Interpretability
papers.research_question: Can mechanistic interpretability extract scientific knowledge from neural networks trained on physics data, and can such insights align with human-derived domain knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that mechanistic interpretability can extract scientifically meaningful representations from neural networks trained on nuclear physics data, aligning with human-derived concepts like the semi-empirical mass formula and shell model.
papers.conclusion: These findings provide a proof-of-concept that neural networks, when trained on scientific data, can learn useful representations that align with human knowledge, opening exciting possibilities for future research on richer data and more complex tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Embeddings of proton and neutron numbers exhibit a helix structure that encodes nuclear physics concepts like the volume and asymmetry terms.
The orderedness of embeddings along the first principal component correlates with generalization performance.
Penultimate layer features correspond to terms in the semi-empirical mass formula and nuclear shell model.
Latent space topography reveals the algorithm used by the model for binding energy prediction, geometrically representing the SEMF.
Models trained on nuclear data learn representations similar to those trained on pseudo data from human-derived theory.
papers.limitation:
Interpretability of extracted knowledge is not guaranteed; representations may be complex and not easily distilled into interpretable theories.
Lack of quantitative metrics to assess interpretability.
Symbolic regression from neural features did not yield fully interpretable improvements over human-derived models.
Requires interdisciplinary collaborations and close partnerships between machine learning researchers and domain experts.
future_direction: Applying interpretability to richer data and more complex tasks.
Developing quantitative metrics for interpretability.
Exploring other scientific domains for knowledge extraction.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) promises a path toward fully understanding how neural networks make their predictions. Prior work demonstrates that even when trained to perform simple arithmetic, models can implement a variety of algorithms (sometimes concurrently) depending on initialization and hyperparameters. Does this mean neuron-level interpretability techniques have limited applicability? We argue that high-dimensional neural networks can learn low-dimensional representations of their training data that are useful beyond simply making good predictions. Such representations can be understood through the mechanistic interpretability lens and provide insights that are surprisingly faithful to human-derived domain knowledge. This indicates that such approaches to interpretability can be useful for deriving a new understanding of a problem from models trained to solve it. As a case study, we extract nuclear physics concepts by studying models trained to reproduce nuclear data.

papers.title: DiffusionPID: Interpreting Diffusion via Partial Information Decomposition
papers.research_question: How do individual tokens and their interactions in a text prompt shape the image generated by a text-to-image diffusion model? The paper investigates what diffusion models learn, how they represent visual-semantic relationships, and why they sometimes fail to generalize.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DiffusionPID, a method based on partial information decomposition (PID) to interpret text-to-image diffusion models by decomposing the input prompt into elementary components and analyzing uniqueness, redundancy, and synergy at both image and pixel levels.
papers.conclusion: DiffusionPID allows for a fine-grained understanding of the decision-making process in diffusion models, helping to identify shortcomings and reasons for failures. This understanding can be used to make diffusion models better aligned with human conceptual understanding and to counter their limitations and biases.
papers.key_findings:
DiffusionPID can reveal gender and ethnic biases in diffusion models by showing higher redundancy between stereotypical occupations and specific genders/ethnicities.
The method characterizes word ambiguity and similarity from the model's perspective, showing high synergy for homonyms with correct modifiers and high redundancy for synonyms.
DiffusionPID enables prompt intervention by identifying redundant words whose removal minimally affects the generated image.
The uniqueness maps can localize the most representative features of a concept, such as the bristles of a toothbrush.
The method provides fine-grained insights into model failures, such as confusing co-hyponyms due to high redundancy, leading to fused or missing objects in generations.
papers.limitation:
The method currently computes PID only for two phrases from the prompt, though it can be extended to more variables.
The approach requires access to the diffusion model, making it difficult to apply to closed-source models.
future_direction: Extending PID to more than two input variables.
Computing PID on other, non-diffusion-based models.
Exploring alternative methods of computing PID for closed-source models.
papers.abstract: Text-to-image diffusion models have made significant progress in generating naturalistic images from textual inputs, and demonstrate the capacity to learn and represent complex visual-semantic relationships. While these diffusion models have achieved remarkable success, the underlying mechanisms driving their performance are not yet fully accounted for, with many unanswered questions surrounding what they learn, how they represent visual-semantic relationships, and why they sometimes fail to generalize. Our work presents Diffusion Partial Information Decomposition (DiffusionPID), a novel technique that applies information-theoretic principles to decompose the input text prompt into its elementary components, enabling a detailed examination of how individual tokens and their interactions shape the generated image. We introduce a formal approach to analyze the uniqueness, redundancy, and synergy terms by applying PID to the denoising model at both the image and pixel level. This approach enables us to characterize how individual tokens and their interactions affect the model output. We first present a fine-grained analysis of characteristics utilized by the model to uniquely localize specific concepts, we then apply our approach in bias analysis and show it can recover gender and ethnicity biases. Finally, we use our method to visually characterize word ambiguity and similarity from the model's perspective and illustrate the efficacy of our method for prompt intervention. Our results show that PID is a potent tool for evaluating and diagnosing text-to-image diffusion models.

papers.title: Understanding Representation Dynamics of Diffusion Models via Low-Dimensional Modeling
papers.research_question: What causes the unimodal representation dynamics in diffusion models, and how does it relate to model generalization?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a theoretical explanation for the unimodal representation dynamics in diffusion models, showing it arises from capturing the low-dimensional data structure, and empirically demonstrates that this dynamics indicates model generalization.
papers.conclusion: The unimodal representation dynamics in diffusion models arise from successful capture of low-dimensional data distributions and serve as a reliable indicator of model generalization.
papers.key_findings:
Unimodal representation dynamics emerge when diffusion models successfully capture the underlying low-dimensional data distribution.
The dynamics are driven by an interplay between denoising strength and class confidence across noise levels.
The presence of unimodal dynamics reliably predicts generalization in classification tasks, while memorization leads to monotonic dynamics.
The unimodal pattern becomes less obvious with smaller dataset sizes and transitions to a monotonically decreasing curve in the memorization regime.
Early stopping during training can improve generalization and restore unimodal dynamics in limited data regimes.
papers.abstract: Diffusion models, though originally designed for generative tasks, have demonstrated impressive self-supervised representation learning capabilities. A particularly intriguing phenomenon in these models is the emergence of unimodal representation dynamics, where the quality of learned features peaks at an intermediate noise level. In this work, we conduct a comprehensive theoretical and empirical investigation of this phenomenon. Leveraging the inherent low-dimensionality structure of image data, we theoretically demonstrate that the unimodal dynamic emerges when the diffusion model successfully captures the underlying data distribution. The unimodality arises from an interplay between denoising strength and class confidence across noise scales. Empirically, we further show that, in classification tasks, the presence of unimodal dynamics reliably reflects the generalization of the diffusion model: it emerges when the model generates novel images and gradually transitions to a monotonically decreasing curve as the model begins to memorize the training data.

papers.title: On the Separability of Information in Diffusion Models
papers.research_question: What information is stored in diffusion models, and how is it allocated between reconstructing perceptual details and conditioning on semantic content?
papers.core_contribution: Diffusion models allocate most of their information to reconstructing perceptual details, while semantic conditioning information is small; this separability explains the efficacy of classifier-free guidance.
papers.conclusion: Diffusion models separate information into perceptual and semantic components, with perceptual details dominating the information budget, which explains the behavior of classifier-free guidance.
papers.key_findings:
A large fraction of the total information in diffusion models is committed to reconstructing small-scale perceptual details of images.
The correlations between images and their class labels are informed by semantic content and are largely agnostic to low-level details.
The manifold structure of images causes neural entropy to be large due to the low-dimensional manifold, while mutual information is small.
Classifier-free guidance amplifies mutual information early in the generative process, influencing semantic structure, but tapers out as perceptual details are filled in.
The efficacy of classifier-free guidance is explained by the separability of information into perceptual and semantic components.
papers.limitation:
Neural entropy estimates may deviate from true values due to sparse datasets or insufficient training.
Lack of access to true scores for image distributions limits the ability to validate estimates.
papers.abstract: Diffusion models transform noise into data by injecting information that was captured in their neural network during the training phase. In this paper, we ask: \textit{what} is this information? We find that, in pixel-space diffusion models, (1) a large fraction of the total information in the neural network is committed to reconstructing small-scale perceptual details of the image, and (2) the correlations between images and their class labels are informed by the semantic content of the images, and are largely agnostic to the low-level details. We argue that these properties are intrinsically tied to the manifold structure of the data itself. Finally, we show that these facts explain the efficacy of classifier-free guidance: the guidance vector amplifies the mutual information between images and conditioning signals early in the generative process, influencing semantic structure, but tapers out as perceptual details are filled in.

papers.title: A Controllable Appearance Representation for Flexible Transfer and Editing
papers.research_question: How can we learn a disentangled and interpretable latent representation of material appearance without human-annotated data, and how can we use it for appearance transfer and editing?
papers.core_contribution: We present a self-supervised method that learns a disentangled and interpretable latent representation of material appearance without human-annotated data, and demonstrate its use for appearance transfer and editing.
papers.conclusion: We have presented a self-supervised method for learning a disentangled and interpretable latent space of material appearance, and demonstrated its effectiveness for appearance transfer and editing tasks.
papers.key_findings:
The model learns a 6D disentangled latent space encoding hue, gloss, lightness, and illumination without any labeled data.
The learned representation allows for fine-grained control in appearance transfer and editing tasks.
Quantitative evaluation shows our model outperforms baselines in disentanglement and reconstruction metrics.
The diffusion pipeline conditioned on our latent space enables selective attribute transfer from multiple images and smooth interpolation.
Our method generalizes to real images despite being trained on synthetic data.
papers.limitation:
The appearance encoder is limited to homogeneous, opaque materials and cannot handle very high-frequency or strongly colored lighting.
The decoder has limited generalization to unseen geometries, leading to artifacts in reconstruction.
papers.abstract: We present a method that computes an interpretable representation of material appearance within a highly compact, disentangled latent space. This representation is learned in a self-supervised fashion using a VAE-based model. We train our model with a carefully designed unlabeled dataset, avoiding possible biases induced by human-generated labels. Our model demonstrates strong disentanglement and interpretability by effectively encoding material appearance and illumination, despite the absence of explicit supervision. To showcase the capabilities of such a representation, we leverage it for two proof-of-concept applications: image-based appearance transfer and editing. Our representation is used to condition a diffusion pipeline that transfers the appearance of one or more images onto a target geometry, and allows the user to further edit the resulting appearance. This approach offers fine-grained control over the generated results: thanks to the well-structured compact latent space, users can intuitively manipulate attributes such as hue or glossiness in image space to achieve the desired final appearance.

papers.title: Critical windows: non-asymptotic theory for feature emergence in diffusion models
papers.research_question: Can we prove the existence of critical windows in the reverse process for a rich family of data distributions?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a formal framework for studying critical windows in diffusion models and proves non-asymptotic bounds on these windows for mixtures of strongly log-concave densities, including Gaussian mixtures, showing that diffusion models act as hierarchical samplers.
papers.key_findings:
The paper gives a general characterization of critical windows for mixtures of strongly log-concave distributions in terms of inter- and intra-group separation.
It provides concrete bounds for Gaussian mixtures, showing that critical window endpoints scale logarithmically with distances between component means.
It proves that for hierarchical mixtures, the reverse process makes a discrete sequence of feature decisions, formalizing the hierarchical sampling interpretation.
Synthetic experiments validate the theoretical bounds on Gaussian mixtures.
Preliminary experiments on Stable Diffusion show critical windows for features like color, background, and size, and suggest applications to fairness and privacy.
papers.abstract: We develop theory to understand an intriguing property of diffusion models for image generation that we term critical windows. Empirically, it has been observed that there are narrow time intervals in sampling during which particular features of the final image emerge, e.g. the image class or background color (Ho et al., 2020b; Meng et al., 2022; Choi et al., 2022; Raya & Ambrogioni, 2023; Georgiev et al., 2023; Sclocchi et al., 2024; Biroli et al., 2024). While this is advantageous for interpretability as it implies one can localize properties of the generation to a small segment of the trajectory, it seems at odds with the continuous nature of the diffusion. We propose a formal framework for studying these windows and show that for data coming from a mixture of strongly log-concave densities, these windows can be provably bounded in terms of certain measures of inter- and intra-group separation. We also instantiate these bounds for concrete examples like well-conditioned Gaussian mixtures. Finally, we use our bounds to give a rigorous interpretation of diffusion models as hierarchical samplers that progressively "decide" output features over a discrete sequence of times. We validate our bounds with synthetic experiments. Additionally, preliminary experiments on Stable Diffusion suggest critical windows may serve as a useful tool for diagnosing fairness and privacy violations in real-world diffusion models.

papers.title: Explainable AI in drug discovery: self-interpretable graph neural network for molecular property prediction using concept whitening
papers.research_question: How can concept whitening be adapted to graph neural networks to create self-interpretable models for molecular property prediction in drug discovery, and does this improve both performance and interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: The paper adapts the concept whitening (CW) interpretability method to graph neural networks, enabling self-interpretable QSAR models that align latent space axes with known molecular properties (concepts) and identify relevant structural parts of molecules for predictions.
papers.conclusion: The adaptation of concept whitening to graph neural networks provides an effective framework for building self-interpretable models in drug discovery, offering improved performance and clear insights into the molecular properties driving predictions.
papers.key_findings:
Adding concept whitening layers to GNNs improves classification performance (ROC-AUC) and interpretability on molecular property prediction tasks.
The method successfully identifies which predefined molecular properties (concepts) are most relevant for predictions at different network depths.
Two novel activation modes for CW in GNNs (weighted_topk_pool and topk_pool) are introduced and evaluated.
The choice of normalization layer (BatchNorm, InstanceNorm, LayerNorm, GraphNorm) in the base model affects the performance after adding CW layers.
The method provides both structural (via GNNExplainer) and conceptual explanations for model predictions in drug discovery.

papers.title: Representation Engineering for Large-Language Models: Survey and Research Challenges
papers.research_question: This paper investigates the goals, methods, and challenges of representation engineering as an approach to make large-language models more predictable and controllable.
papers.core_contribution: This paper formalizes the goals and methods of representation engineering, providing a cohesive survey of this emerging discipline and outlining a research agenda for building more predictable and controllable large-language models.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that representation engineering is a promising approach for enhancing LLM transparency and control, and it provides a clear agenda for future research to address current challenges.
papers.key_findings:
Representation engineering uses contrasting inputs to detect and edit high-level representations, offering a top-down approach to model interpretability and control.
It compares favorably with alternative approaches like mechanistic interpretability and prompt-engineering in certain aspects.
Risks include performance degradation, increased compute time, and steerability issues.
The linear representation hypothesis underpins representation engineering, but its strong form may not hold, limiting generalizability.
Future research should focus on dynamic, safe, and personalizable LLMs through representation engineering.
papers.limitation:
Performance decrease, compute time increases, and steerability issues.
The strong linear representation hypothesis may not hold, limiting generalized interventions.
future_direction: Build predictable, dynamic, safe, and personalizable LLMs through representation engineering.
papers.abstract: Large-language models are capable of completing a variety of tasks, but remain unpredictable and intractable. Representation engineering seeks to resolve this problem through a new approach utilizing samples of contrasting inputs to detect and edit high-level representations of concepts such as honesty, harmfulness or power-seeking. We formalize the goals and methods of representation engineering to present a cohesive picture of work in this emerging discipline. We compare it with alternative approaches, such as mechanistic interpretability, prompt-engineering and fine-tuning. We outline risks such as performance decrease, compute time increases and steerability issues. We present a clear agenda for future research to build predictable, dynamic, safe and personalizable LLMs.

papers.title: SAEs $\textit{Can}$ Improve Unlearning: Dynamic Sparse Autoencoder Guardrails for Precision Unlearning in LLMs
papers.research_question: Can Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) be used to significantly improve machine unlearning in LLMs when employed dynamically, addressing the limitations of gradient-based methods?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Dynamic SAE Guardrails (DSG), a novel activation-based unlearning method that uses principled SAE feature selection and a dynamic classifier to achieve precise, efficient, and interpretable knowledge removal, outperforming gradient-based methods.
papers.conclusion: Dynamic SAE Guardrails (DSG) is an effective, efficient, and interpretable method for machine unlearning that addresses key limitations of gradient-based approaches and demonstrates that SAEs can significantly improve unlearning when used dynamically.
papers.key_findings:
DSG achieves a superior balance between forgetting target knowledge and preserving general utility compared to leading gradient-based and static SAE unlearning methods.
DSG offers greater computational efficiency and hyperparameter stability than gradient-based methods, requiring only forward passes and showing robust performance.
DSG demonstrates strong sequential unlearning capability, scalability to larger forget sets, and enhanced resistance to relearning attacks.
DSG is highly data-efficient and can perform zero-shot unlearning by leveraging semantically relevant SAE features identified without task-specific data.
DSG provides interpretable unlearning by targeting specific, semantically coherent SAE features associated with the knowledge to be removed.
papers.abstract: Machine unlearning is a promising approach to improve LLM safety by removing unwanted knowledge from the model. However, prevailing gradient-based unlearning methods suffer from issues such as high computational costs, hyperparameter instability, poor sequential unlearning capability, vulnerability to relearning attacks, low data efficiency, and lack of interpretability. While Sparse Autoencoders are well-suited to improve these aspects by enabling targeted activation-based unlearning, prior approaches underperform gradient-based methods. This work demonstrates that, contrary to these earlier findings, SAEs can significantly improve unlearning when employed dynamically. We introduce $\textbf{Dynamic DAE Guardrails}$ (DSG), a novel method for precision unlearning that leverages principled feature selection and a dynamic classifier. Our experiments show DSG substantially outperforms leading unlearning methods, achieving superior forget-utility trade-offs. DSG addresses key drawbacks of gradient-based approaches for unlearning -- offering enhanced computational efficiency and stability, robust performance in sequential unlearning, stronger resistance to relearning attacks, better data efficiency including zero-shot settings, and more interpretable unlearning.

papers.title: Hierarchically branched diffusion models leverage dataset structure for class-conditional generation
papers.research_question: How can internal hierarchical structure in class-labeled datasets be leveraged to improve class-conditional diffusion models?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes hierarchically branched diffusion models, a novel framework for class-conditional generation that leverages dataset structure, offering advantages in extendability, transmutation, and interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Branched diffusion models are a novel and effective framework for class-conditional generation that leverages inherent dataset structure, with applications particularly in scientific settings.
papers.key_findings:
Branched diffusion models achieve similar or better generative performance compared to state-of-the-art label-guided diffusion models.
Branched models can be efficiently extended to novel classes in a continual-learning setting without catastrophic forgetting.
Branched models enable analogy-based conditional generation (transmutation) between classes, preserving instance-specific features.
The branching structure provides interpretability into class relationships from a generative perspective.
The method is effective across multiple data modalities (images, tabular data, graphs).
papers.abstract: Class-labeled datasets, particularly those common in scientific domains, are rife with internal structure, yet current class-conditional diffusion models ignore these relationships and implicitly diffuse on all classes in a flat fashion. To leverage this structure, we propose hierarchically branched diffusion models as a novel framework for class-conditional generation. Branched diffusion models rely on the same diffusion process as traditional models, but learn reverse diffusion separately for each branch of a hierarchy. We highlight several advantages of branched diffusion models over the current state-of-the-art methods for class-conditional diffusion, including extension to novel classes in a continual-learning setting, a more sophisticated form of analogy-based conditional generation (i.e. transmutation), and a novel interpretability into the generation process. We extensively evaluate branched diffusion models on several benchmark and large real-world scientific datasets spanning many data modalities.

papers.title: Does Transformer Interpretability Transfer to RNNs?
papers.research_question: Does transformer interpretability transfer to RNNs? Specifically, do contrastive activation addition, the tuned lens, and methods for eliciting latent knowledge work on RNNs like Mamba and RWKV?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that popular transformer interpretability methods (contrastive activation addition, the tuned lens, and methods for eliciting latent knowledge) transfer to state-of-the-art RNN architectures, and that the compressed state of RNNs can be used to enhance activation addition for steering.
papers.conclusion: Interpretability tools designed for transformers largely work out-of-the-box for RNNs, with similar performance, and the compressed state of RNNs can be used to enhance activation addition for steering.
papers.key_findings:
Contrastive activation addition (CAA) is effective for steering RNNs, with middle layers showing the greatest effect.
State steering, using the internal state of RNNs, is possible and can be combined with activation steering, though the effects are not additive.
The tuned lens can be applied to RNNs, with perplexity decreasing monotonically with depth, similar to transformers.
Linear probes trained on 'Alice' contexts can predict the correct answer in 'Bob' contexts for RNNs, similar to transformers.
papers.limitation: The work did not explore mechanistic or circuit-based interpretability tools, focusing instead on representation-based methods.
future_direction: Further exploration of the RNN state for extracting latent knowledge or predictions.
Examination of the applicability of mechanistic interpretability approaches to RNNs.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in recurrent neural network architectures, such as Mamba and RWKV, have enabled RNNs to match or exceed the performance of equal-size transformers in terms of language modeling perplexity and downstream evaluations, suggesting that future systems may be built on completely new architectures. In this paper, we examine if selected interpretability methods originally designed for transformer language models will transfer to these up-and-coming recurrent architectures. Specifically, we focus on steering model outputs via contrastive activation addition, on eliciting latent predictions via the tuned lens, and eliciting latent knowledge from models fine-tuned to produce false outputs under certain conditions. Our results show that most of these techniques are effective when applied to RNNs, and we show that it is possible to improve some of them by taking advantage of RNNs' compressed state.

papers.title: Comparing the latent features of universal machine-learning interatomic potentials
papers.research_question: How do different universal machine-learning interatomic potentials (uMLIPs) encode chemical information in their latent features, and how do these encodings compare across models, training datasets, and training strategies?
papers.core_contribution: This paper systematically analyzes the latent features of universal machine-learning interatomic potentials (uMLIPs) using feature reconstruction errors, revealing that different models encode chemical information in distinct ways and that these differences can be quantified.
papers.conclusion: Predictive accuracy alone is insufficient to characterize atomistic ML models; feature reconstruction error metrics provide a principled foundation for more transparent, interpretable, and robust model design.
papers.key_findings:
uMLIPs encode the chemical space in significantly distinct ways, with substantial cross-model feature reconstruction errors.
When variants of the same model architecture are considered, trends become dependent on the dataset, target, and training protocol.
Fine-tuning of a uMLIP retains a strong pre-training bias in the latent features.
Atom-level features can be compressed into global structure-level features via concatenation of progressive cumulants, each adding significantly new information.
Backbone features contain more information than last-layer features and are more consistent across models.
papers.abstract: The past few years have seen the development of ``universal'' machine-learning interatomic potentials (uMLIPs) capable of approximating the ground-state potential energy surface across a wide range of chemical structures and compositions with reasonable accuracy. While these models differ in the architecture and the dataset used, they share the ability to compress a staggering amount of chemical information into descriptive latent features. Herein, we systematically analyze what the different uMLIPs have learned by quantitatively assessing the relative information content of their latent features with feature reconstruction errors, and observing how the trends are affected by the choice of training set and training protocol. We find that uMLIPs encode the chemical space in significantly distinct ways, with substantial cross-model feature reconstruction errors. When variants of the same model architecture are considered, trends become dependent on the dataset, target, and training protocol of choice. We also observe that fine-tuning of a uMLIP retains a strong pre-training bias in the latent features. Finally, we discuss how atom-level features, which are directly output by MLIPs, can be compressed into global structure-level features via concatenation of progressive cumulants, each adding significantly new information about the variability across the atomic environments within a given system.

papers.title: Uncovering Emergent Physics Representations Learned In-Context by Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do large language models implicitly learn physics during in-context learning, and do recognizable physical quantities emerge as distinct features in their internal representations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that large language models can learn to forecast physical dynamics via in-context learning, and that energy-related features emerge in their residual stream activations, which are causally important for accurate predictions.
papers.conclusion: The results demonstrate that LLMs can internalize physical concepts like energy during in-context learning, suggesting transformer architectures can internalize abstract reasoning priors similar to human abstraction.
papers.key_findings:
Prediction accuracy for physical dynamics forecasting improves with longer context length.
Sparse activations from sparse autoencoders (SAEs) applied to residual streams correlate with energy quantities (total, kinetic, potential).
The correlation between sparse activations and energy is context-dependent and increases with longer contexts, especially for chaotic systems.
Intervention experiments ablating energy-correlated sparse activations degrade prediction accuracy, indicating their functional role.
Energy-related features are most prominently captured in the middle layers of the transformer.
papers.limitation: The study uses raw trajectory values as the sole input modality without external instructions or prompting strategies, leaving open whether chain-of-thought or structured prompts would strengthen correlations.
future_direction: Explore physics concepts beyond classical mechanics.
Investigate more human-aligned tasks such as answering conceptual questions from physics exams.
Leverage physics-informed tasks to understand internal mechanisms of large-scale models and advance LLM-based agents for physically realistic environments.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit impressive in-context learning (ICL) abilities, enabling them to solve wide range of tasks via textual prompts alone. As these capabilities advance, the range of applicable domains continues to expand significantly. However, identifying the precise mechanisms or internal structures within LLMs that allow successful ICL across diverse, distinct classes of tasks remains elusive. Physics-based tasks offer a promising testbed for probing this challenge. Unlike synthetic sequences such as basic arithmetic or symbolic equations, physical systems provide experimentally controllable, real-world data based on structured dynamics grounded in fundamental principles. This makes them particularly suitable for studying the emergent reasoning behaviors of LLMs in a realistic yet tractable setting. Here, we mechanistically investigate the ICL ability of LLMs, especially focusing on their ability to reason about physics. Using a dynamics forecasting task in physical systems as a proxy, we evaluate whether LLMs can learn physics in context. We first show that the performance of dynamics forecasting in context improves with longer input contexts. To uncover how such capability emerges in LLMs, we analyze the model's residual stream activations using sparse autoencoders (SAEs). Our experiments reveal that the features captured by SAEs correlate with key physical variables, such as energy. These findings demonstrate that meaningful physical concepts are encoded within LLMs during in-context learning. In sum, our work provides a novel case study that broadens our understanding of how LLMs learn in context.

papers.title: Towards a Mechanistic Explanation of Diffusion Model Generalization
papers.research_question: How do diffusion models generalize? What is the mechanism behind their generalization behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes that diffusion model generalization arises from local denoising operations and introduces a training-free patch-based denoiser (PSPC) that mimics network denoisers, providing evidence for this mechanism.
papers.conclusion: A significant portion of the generalization behavior of image diffusion models arises from a mechanism substantially similar to time-varying patch denoising and compositing operations.
papers.key_findings:
Network denoisers across different architectures deviate from the optimal denoiser in similar ways, indicating a shared inductive bias.
Network denoisers exhibit a local inductive bias, with gradients concentrated around output pixels.
Patch posterior means approximate network denoiser patches well, especially for small and large noise levels.
The proposed PSPC denoiser, which aggregates patch posterior means, produces outputs visually similar to neural network denoisers.
PSPC samples share structural similarity with network samples, though with some artifacts due to compounding errors.
papers.limitation: PSPC-Flex samples have visual artifacts and compounding errors lead to suboptimal final sample quality compared to neural network denoisers.
papers.abstract: We propose a simple, training-free mechanism which explains the generalization behaviour of diffusion models. By comparing pre-trained diffusion models to their theoretically optimal empirical counterparts, we identify a shared local inductive bias across a variety of network architectures. From this observation, we hypothesize that network denoisers generalize through localized denoising operations, as these operations approximate the training objective well over much of the training distribution. To validate our hypothesis, we introduce novel denoising algorithms which aggregate local empirical denoisers to replicate network behaviour. Comparing these algorithms to network denoisers across forward and reverse diffusion processes, our approach exhibits consistent visual similarity to neural network outputs, with lower mean squared error than previously proposed methods.

papers.title: MolReasoner: Toward Effective and Interpretable Reasoning for Molecular LLMs
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown impressive performance across various domains, but their ability to perform molecular reasoning remains underexplored. Existing methods mostly rely on general-purpose prompting, which lacks domain-specific molecular semantics, or fine-tuning, which faces challenges in interpretability and reasoning depth, often leading to structural and textual hallucinations. To address these issues, we introduce MolReasoner, a two-stage framework that transitions LLMs from memorization to high-fidelity chemical reasoning. In the Mol-SFT stage, knowledge-enhanced Chain-of-Thought (CoT) data provides a strong foundation, while the Mol-RL stage refines reasoning using a novel, task-adaptive reward system to mitigate hallucinations. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that MolReasoner significantly outperforms a wide range of strong baselines in both molecule generation and captioning tasks. Further analyses highlight the framework's synergistic design and its ability to produce more interpretable outputs. Our work presents a principled and effective new approach for advancing high-fidelity molecular reasoning.

papers.title: Cones: Concept Neurons in Diffusion Models for Customized Generation
papers.research_question: Does the parameter space of diffusion models contain concept neurons that correspond to specific subjects, similar to human brains?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals concept neurons in diffusion models that control specific subjects, enabling customized generation by manipulating these neurons.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that concept neurons in diffusion models enable effective customized and multi-subject generation with superior visual quality and storage efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
Concept neurons in diffusion models can be identified using gradient-based methods.
Shutting concept neurons generates the corresponding subject in different contexts.
Concept neurons exhibit additivity, allowing concatenation for multi-subject generation.
Fine-tuning based on concatenated neurons enhances multi-concept capability.
Concept neurons are sparse, reducing storage consumption compared to previous methods.
papers.abstract: Human brains respond to semantic features of presented stimuli with different neurons. It is then curious whether modern deep neural networks admit a similar behavior pattern. Specifically, this paper finds a small cluster of neurons in a diffusion model corresponding to a particular subject. We call those neurons the concept neurons. They can be identified by statistics of network gradients to a stimulation connected with the given subject. The concept neurons demonstrate magnetic properties in interpreting and manipulating generation results. Shutting them can directly yield the related subject contextualized in different scenes. Concatenating multiple clusters of concept neurons can vividly generate all related concepts in a single image. A few steps of further fine-tuning can enhance the multi-concept capability, which may be the first to manage to generate up to four different subjects in a single image. For large-scale applications, the concept neurons are environmentally friendly as we only need to store a sparse cluster of int index instead of dense float32 values of the parameters, which reduces storage consumption by 90\% compared with previous subject-driven generation methods. Extensive qualitative and quantitative studies on diverse scenarios show the superiority of our method in interpreting and manipulating diffusion models.

papers.title: On the flow matching interpretability
papers.research_question: How can we make the intermediate steps of flow matching models interpretable by constraining them to traverse physically meaningful states?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a framework to make flow matching interpretable by constraining each flow step to correspond to equilibrium states of a physical process, demonstrated on the 2D Ising model where steps represent thermal transitions.
papers.conclusion: The paper addresses the challenge of interpreting diffusion steps in flow-matching models by constraining trajectories to physically meaningful transitions, demonstrating preserved physical fidelity with computational speedups over Monte Carlo methods and correct capture of phase transitions and critical phenomena.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed method preserves physical fidelity while outperforming Monte Carlo generation in speed for larger lattices.
Each vector field update represents a meaningful stepwise transition in the 2D Ising model's latent space.
The learned decoder generates configurations that closely resemble true physical behavior, especially near the critical temperature.
The method correctly captures phase transitions and critical phenomena.
The approach transforms abstract flow evolution into concrete, physically-grounded dynamics.
future_direction: Applying the framework to different diffusion models and other physical systems.
papers.abstract: Generative models based on flow matching have demonstrated remarkable success in various domains, yet they suffer from a fundamental limitation: the lack of interpretability in their intermediate generation steps. In fact these models learn to transform noise into data through a series of vector field updates, however the meaning of each step remains opaque. We address this problem by proposing a general framework constraining each flow step to be sampled from a known physical distribution. Flow trajectories are mapped to (and constrained to traverse) the equilibrium states of the simulated physical process. We implement this approach through the 2D Ising model in such a way that flow steps become thermal equilibrium points along a parametric cooling schedule. Our proposed architecture includes an encoder that maps discrete Ising configurations into a continuous latent space, a flow-matching network that performs temperature-driven diffusion, and a projector that returns to discrete Ising states while preserving physical constraints. We validate this framework across multiple lattice sizes, showing that it preserves physical fidelity while outperforming Monte Carlo generation in speed as the lattice size increases. In contrast with standard flow matching, each vector field represents a meaningful stepwise transition in the 2D Ising model's latent space. This demonstrates that embedding physical semantics into generative flows transforms opaque neural trajectories into interpretable physical processes.

papers.title: Designing Role Vectors to Improve LLM Inference Behaviour
papers.research_question: Can we identify specific latent role directions within the activation space that lead to improved performance on objective tasks? Do these directions effectively impersonate the role of interest? Does eliminating these directions degrade performance?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces role vectors as a method to steer LLM behavior by manipulating internal activations, showing that this can improve performance in domain-specific tasks.
papers.conclusion: Role vectors offer a promising pathway for achieving more controllable behaviour in large language models.
papers.key_findings:
Role vectors can steer models to improve performance in target domains.
Larger models show more interpretable role directions.
Only a subset of directions align with intended roles.
Ablating role directions can degrade performance in target domains.
Steering effects are sensitive to model scale and intervention depth.
papers.limitation:
Results might differ in untested models, especially larger ones.
Lack of a complete mechanistic explanation of the phenomenon.
Uncertain semantic interpretation of the identified directions.
Potential degradation in performance in unrelated tasks.
Possible reinforcement of biases or over-confidence.
future_direction: Using Activation Patching (Causal Mediation Analysis) techniques with SAE features to better explain the phenomenon.
Exploring additional analytical dimensions and potential biases.
papers.abstract: The influence of personas on Large Language Models (LLMs) has been widely studied, yet their direct impact on performance remains uncertain. This work explores a novel approach to guiding LLM behaviour through role vectors, an alternative to persona-based prompting. We construct 29 role vectors derived from model activations and evaluate their impact on benchmark performance across multiple domains. Our analysis investigates whether these vectors can effectively steer models toward domain-specific expertise. We measure two key interventions: (i) activation addition, which reinforces role-specific directions, and (ii) directional ablation, which removes them. Results on well-established benchmarks indicate that role vectors do, in fact, influence model behaviour, improving task performance in relevant domains while marginally affecting unrelated tasks. This, in turn, suggests that manipulating internal model representations has a greater impact on outcomes than persona-based prompting.

papers.title: Can abstract concepts from LLM improve SLM performance?
papers.research_question: Can the sophisticated concepts learned by large, powerful models be extracted and used to enhance smaller language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a cross-architecture framework to transfer conceptual knowledge (steering vectors) from a large source model to a smaller target model during inference, and introduces inference-time scaling to dynamically adjust steering intensity, leading to performance improvements without fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: The proposed cross-architecture framework effectively transfers conceptual knowledge via steering vectors, acting as a 'conceptual booster' to enhance smaller, more efficient models without costly fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
Steering vectors extracted from a large source model can be transferred to smaller target models from different architectural families, leading to consistent performance improvements across diverse reasoning tasks.
The performance gains are architecture-agnostic, observed across various model families (Llama, Gemma, Qwen) and datasets (GSM8K, MATH, ARC-C).
Inference-time scaling (running the model across a range of steering coefficients and taking the mode) provides an additional performance uplift, with gains of 7-15% for the smallest model (Qwen3-0.6B).
The steering vectors are architecture-specific, with negligible correlation between the primary directions of variance extracted from different parent models.
Performance is robust at lower steering intensities (λ <= 0.3) but degrades at higher values, and the robustness varies with child model architecture (e.g., Gemma models are more resilient than Llama models).
papers.limitation:
The framework uses a greedy n->n layer mapping between source and target models, which is sub-optimal. The optimal alignment of concepts across different network depths remains an open question.
Using a single λ value for the entire model is greedy and depends on the validation dataset; in reality, λ should be a function of model depth and layer index.
future_direction: Exploring a more sophisticated, cross-architecture layer-mapping strategy.
Dynamically figuring out λ per layer instead of using a single value for the entire model.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel at diverse tasks, but their deployment on resource-constrained devices remains challenging. Existing methods like quantization, pruning, and distillation can reduce memory footprint but often demand extensive experimentation and careful infrastructure design. Leveraging existing techniques for extracting high-level concepts (represented as steering vectors) from larger models, we investigate their transferability to smaller language models (SLM) during inference. We demonstrate through extensive experimentation that these concepts can be effectively transferred to smaller models, irrespective of their family (e.g., Phi, Llama, Qwen), leading to performance improvements across a wide range of tasks. Furthermore, we introduce inference-time scaling to enhance performance by dynamically adjusting the steering intensity which has resulted in a 7-15\% of accuracy improvement for Qwen3-0.6B.

papers.title: Unlocking General Long Chain-of-Thought Reasoning Capabilities of Large Language Models via Representation Engineering
papers.research_question: Is long chain-of-thought reasoning a general capability encoded in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes GLoRE, a training-free representation engineering method that unlocks general long chain-of-thought reasoning capabilities in LLMs by injecting contrastive reasoning pattern and domain-specific representations.
papers.conclusion: The study reveals that long CoT reasoning is a general capability in LLMs and proposes GLoRE, an effective training-free method to unlock it, advancing interpretable slow-thinking models.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs encode long CoT reasoning as a separate general capability, distinct from vanilla CoTs.
Domain-specific representations are required for effective transfer of long CoT reasoning.
GLoRE outperforms training-free baselines and even supervised fine-tuning in both in-domain and cross-domain scenarios.
GLoRE maintains the same time complexity as zero-shot CoT, being more efficient than few-shot methods.
The method is robust to layer selection, with middle layers being most effective.
papers.limitation:
Method requires access to internal representations, making it infeasible for closed-source LLMs.
Experiments are limited to representative tasks and LLMs due to cost and resource constraints.
papers.abstract: Xinyu Tang, Xiaolei Wang, Zhihao Lv, Yingqian Min, Xin Zhao, Binbin Hu, Ziqi Liu, Zhiqiang Zhang. Proceedings of the 63rd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2025.

papers.title: Beyond Converging Representations A Philosophical Response on the Interpretation Risks of Scientific Foundation Models
papers.research_question: Do scientific foundation models of different modalities, architectures, and training data learn similar internal representations of matter?
papers.core_contribution: Representations learned by nearly sixty scientific foundation models across string-, graph-, 3D atomistic, and protein-based modalities are highly aligned, and they converge as model performance improves, suggesting a common underlying representation of physical reality.
papers.conclusion: Representational alignment serves as a quantitative benchmark for foundation-level generality in scientific models, and current models remain limited by training data and inductive biases.
papers.key_findings:
Models trained on different input modalities (e.g., string encodings and 3D coordinates) show significant representational alignment.
As models improve in energy prediction performance, their representations converge towards those of the best-performing models.
Local (CKNNA) and global (dCor) alignment metrics show consistent trends, indicating robust representational similarity.
Intrinsic dimensionality (Id) of embeddings is consistent across models for a given dataset, suggesting a universal low-dimensional structure.
For in-distribution data, high-performing models align closely while weak models diverge; for out-of-distribution data, most models collapse to a low-information representation.
papers.limitation: Today's models remain limited by training data and inductive bias and do not yet encode truly universal structure.
future_direction: Using representational alignment as a quantitative benchmark for foundation-level generality in scientific models.
Tracking the emergence of universal representations of matter as models scale.
Selecting and distilling models whose learned representations transfer best across modalities, domains of matter, and scientific tasks.
papers.abstract: Machine learning models of vastly different modalities and architectures are being trained to predict the behavior of molecules, materials, and proteins. However, it remains unclear whether they learn similar internal representations of matter. Understanding their latent structure is essential for building scientific foundation models that generalize reliably beyond their training domains. Although representational convergence has been observed in language and vision, its counterpart in the sciences has not been systematically explored. Here, we show that representations learned by nearly sixty scientific models, spanning string-, graph-, 3D atomistic, and protein-based modalities, are highly aligned across a wide range of chemical systems. Models trained on different datasets have highly similar representations of small molecules, and machine learning interatomic potentials converge in representation space as they improve in performance, suggesting that foundation models learn a common underlying representation of physical reality. We then show two distinct regimes of scientific models: on inputs similar to those seen during training, high-performing models align closely and weak models diverge into local sub-optima in representation space; on vastly different structures from those seen during training, nearly all models collapse onto a low-information representation, indicating that today's models remain limited by training data and inductive bias and do not yet encode truly universal structure. Our findings establish representational alignment as a quantitative benchmark for foundation-level generality in scientific models. More broadly, our work can track the emergence of universal representations of matter as models scale, and for selecting and distilling models whose learned representations transfer best across modalities, domains of matter, and scientific tasks.

papers.title: Dissecting Role Cognition in Medical LLMs via Neuronal Ablation
papers.research_question: Whether role prompts induce distinct, role-specific cognitive processes in LLMs or merely modify linguistic style.
papers.core_contribution: Role-playing prompts in LLMs do not induce role-specific reasoning pathways; they only affect surface-level linguistic style without altering the core decision-making mechanisms.
papers.conclusion: Role-playing prompts primarily alter language style rather than enabling models to replicate the cognitive processes of real doctors, highlighting the limitations of current methods for building reliable cognitive agents in medical AI.
papers.key_findings:
Role-playing prompts do not significantly improve the medical reasoning accuracy of LLMs across multiple datasets and model scales.
Neuron ablation experiments show similar performance degradation across different roles, indicating a lack of role-specific cognitive pathways.
Representation analysis (CKA, PCA) reveals high similarity and overlapping clusters in hidden states across different roles, showing no hierarchical cognitive differentiation.
Jensen-Shannon Divergence analysis shows role effects are concentrated in early to middle layers and attenuate with depth, not affecting deeper reasoning structures.
Current Prompt-Based Role Playing (PBRP) methods fail to replicate the cognitive complexity and differentiated reasoning strategies of real-world medical professionals.
future_direction: Developing models that go beyond language imitation and incorporate cognitive modeling techniques.
Integrating domain-specific knowledge into the training process and designing systems that can simulate the reasoning strategies of different medical professionals.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have gained significant traction in medical decision support systems, particularly in the context of medical question answering and role-playing simulations. A common practice, Prompt-Based Role Playing (PBRP), instructs models to adopt different clinical roles (e.g., medical students, residents, attending physicians) to simulate varied professional behaviors. However, the impact of such role prompts on model reasoning capabilities remains unclear. This study introduces the RP-Neuron-Activated Evaluation Framework(RPNA) to evaluate whether role prompts induce distinct, role-specific cognitive processes in LLMs or merely modify linguistic style. We test this framework on three medical QA datasets, employing neuron ablation and representation analysis techniques to assess changes in reasoning pathways. Our results demonstrate that role prompts do not significantly enhance the medical reasoning abilities of LLMs. Instead, they primarily affect surface-level linguistic features, with no evidence of distinct reasoning pathways or cognitive differentiation across clinical roles. Despite superficial stylistic changes, the core decision-making mechanisms of LLMs remain uniform across roles, indicating that current PBRP methods fail to replicate the cognitive complexity found in real-world medical practice. This highlights the limitations of role-playing in medical AI and emphasizes the need for models that simulate genuine cognitive processes rather than linguistic imitation.We have released the related code in the following repository:https: //github.com/IAAR-Shanghai/RolePlay_LLMDoctor

papers.title: Evaluating Synthetic Activations composed of SAE Latents in GPT-2
papers.research_question: Do synthetic activations composed of SAE latents behave like real (model-generated) activations in terms of directional sensitivity and activation plateaus? What properties of SAE latents are important for this?
papers.core_contribution: Synthetic activations composed of SAE latents can approximate real activations in directional sensitivity when controlling for sparsity and cosine similarity, but they fail to reproduce activation plateaus, indicating that real activations have additional structure beyond a simple bag of latents.
papers.conclusion: Model-generated activations cannot be explained by simple 'bags of SAE latents'; leveraging statistical and geometric properties of SAE latents helps create synthetic activations more similar to real ones in sensitivity, but these synthetic activations lack the characteristic activation plateaus, suggesting additional latent properties influence model computation.
papers.key_findings:
The 'bag of SAE latents' approach is insufficient to produce synthetic activations that resemble real activations.
Sparsity of the top SAE latent, relative latent activations, and cosine similarity between active latents and the top latent are important for synthetic activations to behave like real activations in sensitivity experiments.
Synthetic activations do not exhibit activation plateaus like real activations do.
SAE reconstructions of real activations behave similarly to real activations, indicating that SAE reconstruction error is not the main cause of the discrepancy.
The model is more sensitive to perturbations towards real activations than random directions, and synthetic-structured activations are more similar to real activations than synthetic-baseline activations in sensitivity experiments.
papers.limitation:
The heuristics for constructing synthetic activations leave room for improvement, as evidenced by the gap between them and model-generated activations, especially for activation plateaus.
The method uses cosine similarity between SAE latents to capture geometric relationships but does not account for latent co-occurrence and other relationships.
The synthetic activations do not match the cosine similarity distribution of SAE latents in model-generated activations closely.
The method leverages information from the base activation to construct synthetic activations (though verified that using a different activation does not change results).
The L2 distance curves exhibit significant variability, impacting the effectiveness of the maximum slope metric; more robust metrics could produce clearer results.
The study focuses solely on one layer of GPT2-small and perturbations confined to the final token position; generalizability to other layers, models, SAEs, and context lengths is not established.
future_direction: Developing better approaches to constructing synthetic activations that perform better in both experimental settings.
Checking for the existence of thresholds below which the model output does not respond to changes in latent activations.
Case studies looking at model sensitivity to perturbations in directions created using interpretable SAE latents and taking context into account.
papers.abstract: Sparse Auto-Encoders (SAEs) are commonly employed in mechanistic interpretability to decompose the residual stream into monosemantic SAE latents. Recent work demonstrates that perturbing a model's activations at an early layer results in a step-function-like change in the model's final layer activations. Furthermore, the model's sensitivity to this perturbation differs between model-generated (real) activations and random activations. In our study, we assess model sensitivity in order to compare real activations to synthetic activations composed of SAE latents. Our findings indicate that synthetic activations closely resemble real activations when we control for the sparsity and cosine similarity of the constituent SAE latents. This suggests that real activations cannot be explained by a simple "bag of SAE latents" lacking internal structure, and instead suggests that SAE latents possess significant geometric and statistical properties. Notably, we observe that our synthetic activations exhibit less pronounced activation plateaus compared to those typically surrounding real activations.

papers.title: Measuring and Guiding Monosemanticity
papers.research_question: How can we systematically measure and improve the monosemanticity (single-concept encoding) of feature representations in large language models, specifically within Sparse Autoencoders?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces the Feature Monosemanticity Score (FMS), a novel metric for quantifying monosemanticity in latent representations, and proposes Guided Sparse Autoencoders (G-SAE), a method that uses latent conditioning during training to enforce isolated, monosemantic feature representations, improving interpretability and control.
papers.conclusion: The introduced FMS metric and G-SAE method provide actionable guidelines for advancing mechanistic interpretability and control of LLMs by enabling reliable measurement and enforcement of monosemantic feature representations.
papers.key_findings:
G-SAE achieves significantly higher FMS scores than vanilla SAEs, indicating stronger feature monosemanticity, localization, and disentanglement.
G-SAE enables more effective and precise concept detection (e.g., toxicity, writing style, privacy attributes) compared to unsupervised SAEs.
Steering using G-SAE's decoder vectors allows for fine-grained control over model outputs (e.g., reducing toxicity, altering writing style) with less quality degradation than baseline methods.
The proposed FMS metric reveals critical shortcomings in the monosemanticity of features learned by standard, unsupervised SAEs.
papers.limitation:
The training of G-SAE requires labeled data for the target concepts, which may not always be available.
The method could be misused for adversarial steering to amplify undesirable model behaviors.
papers.abstract: There is growing interest in leveraging mechanistic interpretability and controllability to better understand and influence the internal dynamics of large language models (LLMs). However, current methods face fundamental challenges in reliably localizing and manipulating feature representations. Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have recently emerged as a promising direction for feature extraction at scale, yet they, too, are limited by incomplete feature isolation and unreliable monosemanticity. To systematically quantify these limitations, we introduce Feature Monosemanticity Score (FMS), a novel metric to quantify feature monosemanticity in latent representation. Building on these insights, we propose Guided Sparse Autoencoders (G-SAE), a method that conditions latent representations on labeled concepts during training. We demonstrate that reliable localization and disentanglement of target concepts within the latent space improve interpretability, detection of behavior, and control. Specifically, our evaluations on toxicity detection, writing style identification, and privacy attribute recognition show that G-SAE not only enhances monosemanticity but also enables more effective and fine-grained steering with less quality degradation. Our findings provide actionable guidelines for measuring and advancing mechanistic interpretability and control of LLMs.

papers.title: Modelling Cellular Perturbations with the Sparse Additive Mechanism Shift Variational Autoencoder
papers.research_question: How to model the effects of diverse interventions on cells to characterize unknown biological mechanisms of action, combining compositionality, disentanglement, and interpretability for perturbation models?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SAMS-VAE, a generative model that combines sparsity, compositionality, and disentanglement for perturbation modeling, demonstrating improved predictive performance and interpretability on single-cell sequencing data.
papers.conclusion: SAMS-VAE is a useful model for perturbational screening data, with improved predictive performance and ability to recover factors correlated with biological mechanisms, and may aid in scientific discovery.
papers.key_findings:
SAMS-VAE with correlated inference achieves the best test IWELBO and average treatment effect correlation.
SAMS-VAE's latent mask is more predictive of annotated biological pathways than SVAE+.
SAMS-VAE and CPA-VAE perform well on out-of-distribution combinatorial tasks and in low-data settings.
SAMS-VAE improves prediction of nonlinear genetic interactions over a naive linear model.
Correlated inference strategies (correlated zbasal and correlated E) improve model performance.
papers.limitation: The prior on the mask may not enforce sparsity as desired when sample size increases, requiring adjustment of the prior strength to achieve desired sparsity.
future_direction: Studying how perturbations interact and compose in more complex fashion.
Incorporating different forms of prior knowledge into such systems.
papers.abstract: Generative models of observations under interventions have been a vibrant topic of interest across machine learning and the sciences in recent years. For example, in drug discovery, there is a need to model the effects of diverse interventions on cells in order to characterize unknown biological mechanisms of action. We propose the Sparse Additive Mechanism Shift Variational Autoencoder, SAMS-VAE, to combine compositionality, disentanglement, and interpretability for perturbation models. SAMS-VAE models the latent state of a perturbed sample as the sum of a local latent variable capturing sample-specific variation and sparse global variables of latent intervention effects. Crucially, SAMS-VAE sparsifies these global latent variables for individual perturbations to identify disentangled, perturbation-specific latent subspaces that are flexibly composable. We evaluate SAMS-VAE both quantitatively and qualitatively on a range of tasks using two popular single cell sequencing datasets. In order to measure perturbation-specific model-properties, we also introduce a framework for evaluation of perturbation models based on average treatment effects with links to posterior predictive checks. SAMS-VAE outperforms comparable models in terms of generalization across in-distribution and out-of-distribution tasks, including a combinatorial reasoning task under resource paucity, and yields interpretable latent structures which correlate strongly to known biological mechanisms. Our results suggest SAMS-VAE is an interesting addition to the modeling toolkit for machine learning-driven scientific discovery.

papers.title: The Representation and Recall of Interwoven Structured Knowledge in LLMs: A Geometric and Layered Analysis
papers.research_question: How do LLMs encode interwoven scientific knowledge, and do they reflect geometric structures like the periodic table?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs encode scientific knowledge in geometric structures, such as a 3D spiral aligning with the periodic table, representing knowledge as interwoven manifolds rather than isolated facts.
papers.conclusion: LLMs develop internal representations that reflect the structured geometry of scientific knowledge, representing symbolic knowledge as geometry-aware, interwoven manifolds.
papers.key_findings:
A 3D spiral structure is observed in hidden states that aligns with the periodic table.
Middle layers encode continuous attributes enabling indirect recall, while deeper layers sharpen categorical distinctions.
Linguistic context increasingly shapes representations in later layers.
Middle layers have strong linear associations between related attributes, which weaken in deeper layers.
papers.limitation:
Prompts are focused on chemical elements and may not extend to domains with more abstract features.
Hypothesis-driven validation may oversimplify LLMs' non-linear interactions.
