However, MoLMs can encode and propagate inaccuracies due to outdated web-mined training corpora or malicious manipulation, jeopardizing downstream discovery pipelines. While knowledge editing has been explored for general-domain AI, its application to MoLMs remains uncharted, presenting unique challenges due to the multifaceted and interdependent nature of molecular knowledge. In this paper, we take the first step toward MoLM editing for two critical tasks: molecule-to-caption generation and caption-to-molecule generation. To address molecule-specific challenges, we propose MolEdit, a powerful framework that enables targeted modifications while preserving unrelated molecular knowledge. MolEdit combines a Multi-Expert Knowledge Adapter that routes edits to specialized experts for different molecular facets with an Expertise-Aware Editing Switcher that activates the adapters only when input closely matches the stored edits across all expertise, minimizing interference with unrelated knowledge. To systematically evaluate editing performance, we introduce MEBench, a comprehensive benchmark assessing multiple dimensions, including Reliability (accuracy of the editing), Locality (preservation of irrelevant knowledge), and Generality (robustness to reformed queries). Across extensive experiments on two popular MoLM backbones, MolEdit delivers up to 18.8% higher Reliability and 12.0% better Locality than baselines while maintaining efficiency. The code is available at: https://github.com/LzyFischer/MolEdit.

papers.title: ExpertSteer: Intervening in LLMs through Expert Knowledge
papers.research_question: How can we guide LLMs to follow desired behaviors during inference by leveraging external expert models for activation steering, overcoming limitations of existing methods that rely on the model itself?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes EXPERTSTEER, a method that leverages external expert models to generate steering vectors for activation steering in LLMs, enabling effective knowledge transfer without updating model parameters.
papers.conclusion: EXPERTSTEER is an effective and efficient activation steering method that enables knowledge transfer from any expert model to arbitrary target LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
EXPERTSTEER outperforms existing activation steering methods across diverse tasks and models.
It works effectively in both same-family and cross-family model settings.
RFMs are more effective for feature extraction compared to linear methods like PCA and mean difference.
The choice of expert model is crucial for effective steering.
EXPERTSTEER is computationally efficient.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable capabilities across various tasks, yet guiding them to follow desired behaviours during inference remains a significant challenge. Activation steering offers a promising method to control the generation process of LLMs by modifying their internal activations. However, existing methods commonly intervene in the model's behaviour using steering vectors generated by the model itself, which constrains their effectiveness to that specific model and excludes the possibility of leveraging powerful external expert models for steering. To address these limitations, we propose ExpertSteer, a novel approach that leverages arbitrary specialized expert models to generate steering vectors, enabling intervention in any LLMs. ExpertSteer transfers the knowledge from an expert model to a target LLM through a cohesive four-step process: first aligning representation dimensions with auto-encoders to enable cross-model transfer, then identifying intervention layer pairs based on mutual information analysis, next generating steering vectors from the expert model using Recursive Feature Machines, and finally applying these vectors on the identified layers during inference to selectively guide the target LLM without updating model parameters. We conduct comprehensive experiments using three LLMs on 15 popular benchmarks across four distinct domains. Experiments demonstrate that ExpertSteer significantly outperforms established baselines across diverse tasks at minimal cost.

papers.title: Explainability Techniques for Chemical Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we explain the predictions of chemical language models by attributing importance to individual atoms in the input molecular string?
papers.core_contribution: We propose an explainable AI technique for chemical language models that attributes the importance of individual atoms to the model's predictions by backpropagating relevance through attention scores and gradients, and visualize the importance on the molecular structure.
papers.conclusion: We propose an attribution technique for Transformers operating on molecular string representations, which provides interpretable predictions and allows inspection of the model's learned features for solubility prediction.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed method achieves competitive predictive performance on aqueous and organic solvent solubility prediction tasks.
The visualizations highlight atoms that are important for solubility, which can be validated by chemists.
The model sometimes attributes high relevance to the carbon backbone, which may be due to the pretraining procedure.
The method is applicable to self-attention Transformers and can be extended to other architectures.
papers.limitation:
The method only visualizes atom tokens and does not handle non-atom tokens (e.g., bonds, brackets) in the SMILES string.
The model does not enforce invariance to different SMILES representations of the same molecule.
future_direction: Extend the visualization to non-atom tokens in the SMILES string.
Enforce SMILES invariance in the model through contrastive training.
Apply the explainability technique to other Transformer architectures, such as generative models.
papers.abstract: Explainability techniques are crucial in gaining insights into the reasons behind the predictions of deep learning models, which have not yet been applied to chemical language models. We propose an explainable AI technique that attributes the importance of individual atoms towards the predictions made by these models. Our method backpropagates the relevance information towards the chemical input string and visualizes the importance of individual atoms. We focus on self-attention Transformers operating on molecular string representations and leverage a pretrained encoder for finetuning. We showcase the method by predicting and visualizing solubility in water and organic solvents. We achieve competitive model performance while obtaining interpretable predictions, which we use to inspect the pretrained model.

papers.title: Revealing Token-Level Importance in Conditional Molecular Design Through Kullback–Leibler Divergence
papers.research_question: How can we explain conditional molecular design models by quantifying the influence of property conditions on the generative process to reveal token-level importance?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a method to interpret conditional molecular design models using Kullback-Leibler Divergence to quantify the token-level importance of property conditions during generation.
papers.conclusion: Introduced a novel method for interpreting conditional molecular design models using KL divergence to quantify the influence of property conditions.
future_direction: Analyze how perturbations on the most important tokens affect predicted property values
Compare the explainability method with other approaches in the literature
Assess generalization to other textual- and graph-based molecular representations
papers.abstract: Conditional molecular design using transformer-based models can accelerate drug discovery, but their black-box nature limits interpretability. We propose a method to explain these models by quantifying the influence of property conditions on the generative process. Our approach uses the Kullback–Leibler Divergence to measure the difference between conditional and unconditional output distributions at each generation step. This allows us to identify the token-level importance of a sequence for specific desired conditions.

papers.title: Exploring the Representation Manifolds of Stable Diffusion Through the Lens of Intrinsic Dimension
papers.research_question: How do prompts affect the intrinsic dimension of internal representations in Stable Diffusion?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that prompt choice significantly affects the intrinsic dimension of representations in Stable Diffusion, with correlation to prompt perplexity in bottleneck layers.
papers.conclusion: Intrinsic dimension could be a useful tool for future studies of the impact of different prompts on text-to-image models.
papers.key_findings:
Prompts have a substantial effect on the intrinsic dimension of internal representations, with variations up to 10 dimensions.
Intrinsic dimension in latent representations decreases monotonically during denoising, while in bottleneck representations it forms a U-shaped curve.
In bottleneck layers, intrinsic dimension correlates with prompt perplexity, suggesting that less likely prompts result in higher-dimensional representations.
The dynamics of intrinsic dimension over denoising steps depend on the layer from which representations are extracted.
The time step embedding vector contributes to the increase in intrinsic dimension in bottleneck representations at later denoising steps.
papers.limitation: The correlation between perplexity and intrinsic dimension must be treated with caution, as it is not observed in latent representations.
future_direction: Adapting the experiments to other text-to-image models like DALL-E.
Comparing perplexity scores with actual frequencies of prompt tokens in training data like LAION-5B.
More comprehensive studies of other models that utilize prompts.
papers.abstract: Prompting has become an important mechanism by which users can more effectively interact with many flavors of foundation model. Indeed, the last several years have shown that well-honed prompts can sometimes unlock emergent capabilities within such models. While there has been a substantial amount of empirical exploration of prompting within the community, relatively few works have studied prompting at a mathematical level. In this work we aim to take a first step towards understanding basic geometric properties induced by prompts in Stable Diffusion, focusing on the intrinsic dimension of internal representations within the model. We find that choice of prompt has a substantial impact on the intrinsic dimension of representations at both layers of the model which we explored, but that the nature of this impact depends on the layer being considered. For example, in certain bottleneck layers of the model, intrinsic dimension of representations is correlated with prompt perplexity (measured using a surrogate model), while this correlation is not apparent in the latent layers. Our evidence suggests that intrinsic dimension could be a useful tool for future studies of the impact of different prompts on text-to-image models.

papers.title: Interpretable Diffusion Models with B-cos Networks
papers.research_question: How can text-to-image diffusion models be made inherently interpretable to provide insight into how individual prompt tokens affect the generated image?
papers.core_contribution: This paper integrates B-cos networks into text-to-image diffusion models, providing inherent interpretability and token-level attributions that link output pixels to prompt tokens, enabling the detection of missing concepts in generated images.
papers.conclusion: B-cos networks can be effectively used in text-to-image diffusion models to provide inherent interpretability, with explanations that faithfully capture the alignment between an image and its prompt, enabling the detection of missing concepts.
papers.key_findings:
B-cos networks can be effectively integrated into diffusion models, providing faithful explanations of prompt-image alignment.
The proposed method yields token-level attributions that consistently assign higher relevance scores to semantically meaningful tokens.
The explanations can identify failure cases where the generated image does not align with the prompt, such as a missing object.
The model summary (dynamic linear transformation) effectively captures the underlying computations, as shown by the close match between normalized reconstructions and model outputs.
Using deterministic sampling (DDIM with σ=0) avoids introducing biases that would break the completeness of the B-cos summary.
papers.limitation: The approach currently leads to reduced generative performance (lower image quality) compared to standard diffusion models.
future_direction: Developing methods to overcome the trade-off between interpretability and generative performance.
papers.abstract: Text-to-image diffusion models generate images by iteratively denoising random noise, conditioned on a prompt. While these models have enabled impressive progress in image generation, they often fail to accurately reflect all semantic information described in the prompt -- failures that are difficult to detect automatically. In this work, we introduce a diffusion model architecture built with B-cos modules that offers inherent interpretability. Our approach provides insight into how individual prompt tokens affect the generated image by producing explanations that highlight the pixel regions influenced by each token. We demonstrate that B-cos diffusion models can produce high-quality images while providing meaningful insights into prompt-image alignment.

papers.title: Partnering with Radical AI to Advance Materials Science With Interpretability
papers.core_contribution: This blog announces a partnership between Radical AI and Goodfire to apply interpretability methods to AI-driven materials discovery models, aiming to extract underlying physical and chemical principles for scientific insight and more explainable AI.
papers.conclusion: The collaboration represents a significant step towards interpretable AI that bridges correlation and causation, accelerating materials discovery and fundamental understanding of how AI learns about the physical world.
papers.abstract: This blog announces a partnership between Radical AI and Goodfire to apply interpretability methods to AI-driven materials discovery models, aiming to extract underlying physical and chemical principles for scientific insight and more explainable AI. The collaboration represents a significant step towards interpretable AI that bridges correlation and causation, accelerating materials discovery and fundamental understanding of how AI learns about the physical world.

papers.title: Crystal Graph Convolutional Neural Networks for an Accurate and Interpretable Prediction of Material Properties
papers.research_question: How can we develop a machine learning framework that directly learns material properties from the atomic connection in a crystal, providing both accurate predictions and interpretable chemical insights?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Crystal Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (CGCNN) framework, which directly learns material properties from crystal graphs, achieving DFT-level accuracy for diverse properties and enabling the extraction of local chemical environment contributions for interpretability.
papers.conclusion: The CGCNN framework provides a flexible, accurate, and interpretable method for predicting material properties and extracting design knowledge, as demonstrated by its application to perovskite discovery.
papers.key_findings:
CGCNN achieves prediction accuracy comparable to DFT calculations for eight different material properties using around 10^4 training data points.
The framework is interpretable, allowing extraction of site-specific energy contributions, as demonstrated for perovskite structures.
The learned site energy information can be used to derive empirical rules for material design, significantly reducing the search space for high-throughput screening.
A modified convolution function (Eq. 5) that differentiates interaction strengths between neighbors significantly improves prediction performance over a simpler version (Eq. 4).
CGCNN can predict both continuous properties (e.g., formation energy) and discrete properties (e.g., metal/semiconductor classification) with high accuracy.
papers.limitation: The initial convolution function (Eq. 4) uses a shared weight matrix for all neighbors of an atom, which neglects differences in interaction strength between neighbors.
papers.abstract: The use of machine learning methods for accelerating the design of crystalline materials usually requires manually constructed feature vectors or complex transformation of atom coordinates to input the crystal structure, which either constrains the model to certain crystal types or makes it difficult to provide chemical insights. Here, we develop a crystal graph convolutional neural networks framework to directly learn material properties from the connection of atoms in the crystal, providing a universal and interpretable representation of crystalline materials. Our method provides a highly accurate prediction of density functional theory calculated properties for eight different properties of crystals with various structure types and compositions after being trained with 10^{4} data points. Further, our framework is interpretable because one can extract the contributions from local chemical environments to global properties. Using an example of perovskites, we show how this information can be utilized to discover empirical rules for materials design.

papers.title: Self-Discovering Interpretable Diffusion Latent Directions for Responsible Text-to-Image Generation
papers.research_question: Are there any internal representations associated with inappropriate concepts in the diffusion model-based generation process? Can we manipulate representations to avoid inappropriate content corresponding to a given concept, i.e., to achieve responsible image generation?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a self-supervised approach to find interpretable latent directions in the diffusion model's h-space for any given concept, and uses these vectors to enhance responsible image generation (fairness, safety, and responsible text-enhancing generation).
papers.conclusion: The work contributes to understanding internal representations in diffusion models and facilitates the generation of responsible content, maximizing the utility of high-quality text-to-image generation.
papers.key_findings:
Ethical-related concepts (e.g., gender, safety) exist in the internal semantic space (h-space) of diffusion models.
Manipulating these concept vectors by adding them to the h-space activations can control the corresponding attributes in generated images.
The self-discovery approach effectively identifies concept vectors without requiring labeled data or external models.
The method outperforms existing debiasing and safety approaches on fairness and safety benchmarks.
The learned concept vectors exhibit properties such as interpolation, composition, and generalization to different prompts and objects.
papers.abstract: Diffusion-based models have gained significant popularity for text-to-image generation due to their exceptional image-generation capabilities. A risk with these models is the potential generation of inappropriate content, such as biased or harmful images. However, the underlying reasons for generating such undesired content from the perspective of the diffusion model's internal representation remain unclear. Previous work interprets vectors in an interpretable latent space of diffusion models as semantic concepts. However, existing approaches cannot discover directions for arbitrary concepts, such as those related to inappropriate concepts. In this work, we propose a novel self-supervised approach to find interpretable latent directions for a given concept. With the discovered vectors, we further propose a simple approach to mitigate inappropriate generation. Extensive experiments have been conducted to verify the effectiveness of our mitigation approach, namely, for fair generation, safe generation, and responsible text-enhancing generation. Project page: \url{https://interpretdiffusion.github.io}.

papers.title: DLM-Scope: Mechanistic Interpretability of Diffusion Language Models via Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders (SAEs) be used for mechanistic interpretability in diffusion language models (DLMs), and how do their properties and applications differ from those in autoregressive LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DLM-Scope, the first SAE-based interpretability framework for Diffusion Language Models (DLMs), demonstrating that SAEs can extract interpretable features, enable effective diffusion-time steering, analyze decoding order, and transfer from base to instruction-tuned models.
papers.conclusion: DLM-Scope establishes a foundation for mechanistic interpretability in DLMs and shows the great potential of applying SAEs to DLM-related tasks and algorithms.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs trained on DLMs achieve a favorable sparsity-fidelity trade-off and can even reduce cross-entropy loss when inserted in early layers, a phenomenon absent or weaker in LLMs.
SAE features enable effective diffusion-time interventions (steering) that often outperform single-pass LLM steering.
SAE feature dynamics provide a useful signal for analyzing and correlating with the performance of different DLM decoding-order strategies.
Base-trained SAEs transfer almost losslessly to instruction-tuned DLMs in shallow and middle layers, but not in the deepest layer, indicating tuning-specific changes in deep representations.
future_direction: As DLMs scale, we plan to extend SAEs to more DLMs to better understand and improve models.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have become a standard tool for mechanistic interpretability in autoregressive large language models (LLMs), enabling researchers to extract sparse, human-interpretable features and intervene on model behavior. Recently, as diffusion language models (DLMs) have become an increasingly promising alternative to the autoregressive LLMs, it is essential to develop tailored mechanistic interpretability tools for this emerging class of models. In this work, we present DLM-Scope, the first SAE-based interpretability framework for DLMs, and demonstrate that trained Top-K SAEs can faithfully extract interpretable features. Notably, we find that inserting SAEs affects DLMs differently than autoregressive LLMs: while SAE insertion in LLMs typically incurs a loss penalty, in DLMs it can reduce cross-entropy loss when applied to early layers, a phenomenon absent or markedly weaker in LLMs. Additionally, SAE features in DLMs enable more effective diffusion-time interventions, often outperforming LLM steering. Moreover, we pioneer certain new SAE-based research directions for DLMs: we show that SAEs can provide useful signals for DLM decoding order; and the SAE features are stable during the post-training phase of DLMs. Our work establishes a foundation for mechanistic interpretability in DLMs and shows a great potential of applying SAEs to DLM-related tasks and algorithms.

papers.title: Evaluating Self-Supervised Learning for Molecular Graph Embeddings
papers.research_question: How can we effectively evaluate graph self-supervised learning (GSSL) methods for molecular graph embeddings, given that their broad applicability complicates evaluation and current downstream datasets may not provide a complete picture?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces MOLGRAPH EVAL, a benchmark for evaluating molecular graph embeddings from GSSL methods via a suite of probing tasks, revealing significant inconsistencies between inferences from existing downstream datasets and more nuanced probing.
papers.conclusion: MOLGRAPH EVAL provides a more comprehensive and nuanced evaluation of GSSL methods for molecular graphs, uncovering limitations of current evaluation methodologies that rely solely on downstream task performance.
papers.key_findings:
All GSSL methods improve molecular property prediction (MPP) over random initialization, but the performance gain varies with dataset size.
Rankings of GSSL methods differ between using fixed embeddings (probing) and fine-tuned embeddings, indicating probing alone is not a definitive indicator for fine-tuning performance.
Optimal pre-training hyperparameters for fixed and fine-tuned embeddings often differ, suggesting that probing fixed embeddings may not reflect true downstream performance after fine-tuning.
Randomly initialized embeddings outperform almost every GSSL method on node- and pair-level topological metrics, indicating GSSL methods are not universally better and random features can be useful for local geometry tasks.
Substructure detection performance correlates well with MPP performance, suggesting that GSSL methods' superiority in MPP may be attributed to their capacity for substructure awareness.
papers.limitation:
The benchmark is limited to the nine studied GSSL methods and the molecular datasets used; extending to more methods and datasets is needed for broader conclusions.
Potential ethical concerns include bias and fairness in the datasets, dual use for designing harmful substances, environmental impact of training, and privacy issues.
future_direction: Extend the benchmark to incorporate more GSSL methods and larger datasets (e.g., ZINC15).
Investigate why optimal pre-training configurations for probing and fine-tuning differ.
Explore the reasons behind the strong performance of randomly initialized embeddings on local topological metrics.
papers.abstract: Graph Self-Supervised Learning (GSSL) provides a robust pathway for acquiring embeddings without expert labelling, a capability that carries profound implications for molecular graphs due to the staggering number of potential molecules and the high cost of obtaining labels. However, GSSL methods are designed not for optimisation within a specific domain but rather for transferability across a variety of downstream tasks. This broad applicability complicates their evaluation. Addressing this challenge, we present "Molecular Graph Representation Evaluation" (MOLGRAPHEVAL), generating detailed profiles of molecular graph embeddings with interpretable and diversified attributes. MOLGRAPHEVAL offers a suite of probing tasks grouped into three categories: (i) generic graph, (ii) molecular substructure, and (iii) embedding space properties. By leveraging MOLGRAPHEVAL to benchmark existing GSSL methods against both current downstream datasets and our suite of tasks, we uncover significant inconsistencies between inferences drawn solely from existing datasets and those derived from more nuanced probing. These findings suggest that current evaluation methodologies fail to capture the entirety of the landscape.

papers.title: Generalization of Diffusion Models Arises with a Balanced Representation Space
papers.research_question: What distinguishes memorization from generalization in diffusion models, and how does representation learning explain this phenomenon?
papers.core_contribution: We prove that memorization in diffusion models corresponds to storing raw training data in weights, yielding spiky representations, while generalization arises from learning data statistics, yielding balanced representations. Based on this, we propose representation-based methods for memorization detection and training-free image editing via representation steering.
papers.conclusion: Our results highlight that learning good representations is central to novel and meaningful generative modeling.
papers.key_findings:
Memorization in overparameterized DAEs leads to weights that store individual training samples, producing spiky activations.
Generalization in underparameterized DAEs leads to weights that capture local data statistics, producing balanced activations.
Real-world diffusion models exhibit a hybrid regime due to data imbalance, memorizing scarce clusters and generalizing abundant ones.
Memorized samples can be detected by the spikiness (high standard deviation) of their representations.
Generalized samples are steerable in representation space for controllable editing, while memorized samples are not.
papers.abstract: Diffusion models excel at generating high-quality, diverse samples, yet they risk memorizing training data when overfit to the training objective. We analyze the distinctions between memorization and generalization in diffusion models through the lens of representation learning. By investigating a two-layer ReLU denoising autoencoder (DAE), we prove that (i) memorization corresponds to the model storing raw training samples in the learned weights for encoding and decoding, yielding localized spiky representations, whereas (ii) generalization arises when the model captures local data statistics, producing balanced representations. Furthermore, we validate these theoretical findings on real-world unconditional and text-to-image diffusion models, demonstrating that the same representation structures emerge in deep generative models with significant practical implications. Building on these insights, we propose a representation-based method for detecting memorization and a training-free editing technique that allows precise control via representation steering. Together, our results highlight that learning good representations is central to novel and meaningful generative modeling.

papers.title: Hierarchical Koopman Diffusion: Fast Generation with Interpretable Diffusion Trajectory
papers.research_question: How to achieve both one-step sampling and interpretable generative trajectories in diffusion models, bridging the gap between fast sampling and interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a novel framework that achieves one-step sampling and interpretable generative trajectories by lifting diffusion dynamics into a latent Koopman space with linear operators and a hierarchical structure.
papers.conclusion: HKD bridges the gap between fast sampling and interpretability in diffusion models, paving the way for explainable image synthesis in generative modeling.
papers.key_findings:
HKD achieves competitive one-step generation performance on CIFAR-10 and FFHQ datasets.
The framework provides interpretability through spectral analysis of Koopman operators, revealing a correspondence between spectral components and semantic image attributes.
It enables fine-grained control and editing of the generative process via frequency-aware interventions along the diffusion trajectory.
papers.abstract: Diffusion models have achieved impressive success in high-fidelity image generation but suffer from slow sampling due to their inherently iterative denoising process. While recent one-step methods accelerate inference by learning direct noise-to-image mappings, they sacrifice the interpretability and fine-grained control intrinsic to diffusion dynamics, key advantages that enable applications like editable generation. To resolve this dichotomy, we introduce \textbf{Hierarchical Koopman Diffusion}, a novel framework that achieves both one-step sampling and interpretable generative trajectories. Grounded in Koopman operator theory, our method lifts the nonlinear diffusion dynamics into a latent space where evolution is governed by globally linear operators, enabling closed-form trajectory solutions. This formulation not only eliminates iterative sampling but also provides full access to intermediate states, allowing manual intervention during generation. To model the multi-scale nature of images, we design a hierarchical architecture that disentangles generative dynamics across spatial resolutions via scale-specific Koopman subspaces, capturing coarse-to-fine details systematically. We empirically show that the Hierarchical Koopman Diffusion not only achieves competitive one-step generation performance but also provides a principled mechanism for interpreting and manipulating the generative process through spectral analysis. Our framework bridges the gap between fast sampling and interpretability in diffusion models, paving the way for explainable image synthesis in generative modeling.

papers.title: SliderSpace: Decomposing the Visual Capabilities of Diffusion Models
papers.research_question: Can we automatically discover the visual structure within a diffusion model’s knowledge of a concept, enabling controllable and interpretable directions without manual specification?
papers.core_contribution: SliderSpace is a framework that automatically decomposes diffusion models' visual capabilities into semantically meaningful and controllable directions by performing spectral decomposition in semantic space and aligning low-rank adapters, enabling systematic exploration without manual attribute specification.
papers.conclusion: SliderSpace enables systematic exploration of diffusion models' latent creative space by automatically decomposing their capabilities into semantically meaningful and controllable directions without requiring manual attribute specification.
papers.key_findings:
SliderSpace decomposes high-level concepts into diverse and expressive components, revealing natural axes of variation in the model's understanding.
For artistic style exploration, SliderSpace discovers directions that match or exceed the diversity of manually curated artist lists and are judged more useful by human evaluators.
SliderSpace can reverse mode collapse in distilled diffusion models, restoring diversity while maintaining generation speed.
SliderSpace directions are transferable to related and out-of-domain concepts, indicating they capture fundamental visual transformations.
User studies show that SliderSpace-generated images are perceived as more diverse, useful, and creative compared to baseline methods.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on semantic embeddings introduces biases present in the encoder's training data, which may not capture culturally-specific or nuanced artistic concepts.
The discovery process requires significant computational time (≈2 hours on an A100 GPU), limiting rapid experimentation.
Discovered art directions may not one-to-one match original artists.
future_direction: More careful study on choices of semantic embeddings and their effects on SliderSpace discovery.
Training time optimizations to reduce computational overhead.
Discovery that nudges directions to be aligned with real artists.
papers.abstract: We present SliderSpace, a framework for automatically decomposing the visual capabilities of diffusion models into controllable and human-understandable directions. Unlike existing control methods that require a user to specify attributes for each edit direction individually, SliderSpace discovers multiple interpretable and diverse directions simultaneously from a single text prompt. Each direction is trained as a low-rank adaptor, enabling compositional control and the discovery of surprising possibilities in the model's latent space. Through extensive experiments on state-of-the-art diffusion models, we demonstrate SliderSpace's effectiveness across three applications: concept decomposition, artistic style exploration, and diversity enhancement. Our quantitative evaluation shows that SliderSpace-discovered directions decompose the visual structure of model's knowledge effectively, offering insights into the latent capabilities encoded within diffusion models. User studies further validate that our method produces more diverse and useful variations compared to baselines. Our code, data and trained weights are available at https://sliderspace.baulab.info

papers.title: The Next Five Hurdles What is a Linear Representation? What is a Multidimensional Feature? The Dark Matter of Neural Networks? Attention Pivot Tables Measuring feature sensitivity using dataset filtering
papers.research_question: What are the major hurdles facing mechanistic interpretability, and how can we improve feature analysis and measurement?
papers.core_contribution: This blog post outlines five key hurdles in mechanistic interpretability, refines the concept of linear representations to include multidimensional features, introduces the idea of 'dark matter' features, provides practical guidance for using attention pivot tables, and demonstrates a method to measure feature sensitivity using LLM-assisted dataset filtering.
papers.conclusion: The authors are optimistic about progress in mechanistic interpretability despite challenges, and highlight the need for further research into feature cooperation and improved analysis methods.
papers.key_findings:
Current sparse autoencoder methods may miss many rare features, suggesting a 'dark matter' of neural networks that is difficult to observe.
Linear representations can be mathematically linear even with multidimensional features, requiring a revised definition.
Attention pivot tables reveal interpretable skip-trigrams in one-layer transformers, but their clarity depends on training details and dataset.
Feature sensitivity measured via Claude-filtered datasets shows that individual features often have low sensitivity, and concepts are represented by multiple cooperating features.
Different versions of Claude agree well with each other and with human judgments when rating concept relevance in text snippets.
papers.limitation:
Dictionary learning may be unable to resolve extremely rare features, limiting comprehensiveness.
Features identified by sparse autoencoders often have imperfect sensitivity and specificity, with concepts distributed across multiple features.
Attention pivot table results are sensitive to training hyperparameters and dataset composition, making interpretation unreliable under suboptimal conditions.
future_direction: Developing more efficient dictionary learning algorithms to capture rare features.
Automating the discovery of complementary features that collectively represent concepts.
Further investigation into attention superposition and cross-layer superposition.
papers.abstract: What are the major hurdles facing mechanistic interpretability, and how can we improve feature analysis and measurement? This blog post outlines five key hurdles in mechanistic interpretability, refines the concept of linear representations to include multidimensional features, introduces the idea of 'dark matter' features, provides practical guidance for using attention pivot tables, and demonstrates a method to measure feature sensitivity using LLM-assisted dataset filtering. The authors are optimistic about progress in mechanistic interpretability despite challenges, and highlight the need for further research into feature cooperation and improved analysis methods.

papers.title: Interpretable Diffusion via Information Decomposition
papers.research_question: How can we understand the fine-grained relationships learned by diffusion models between words and parts of an image, and predict the effect of interventions?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that diffusion models admit a tractable information decomposition, allowing fine-grained analysis of relationships between text and image, and applies this to tasks like compositional understanding, object localization, and measuring intervention effects.
papers.conclusion: The information decomposition method expands the usefulness of diffusion models for interpretability and can be applied to various tasks, including biomedical applications.
papers.key_findings:
Diffusion models have better compositional understanding than previously thought, as measured by the ARO benchmark.
Pixel-wise conditional mutual information can localize objects and abstract words in images.
Conditional mutual information correlates with the effect of prompt interventions, whereas attention does not always do so.
papers.limitation:
The method relies on pre-trained diffusion models and may not perfectly align with segmentation tasks.
Dataset biases and ethical concerns exist in the training data.
future_direction: Applying the method to biomedical data like gene expression.
Using the method for circuit analysis in diffusion models.
papers.abstract: Denoising diffusion models enable conditional generation and density modeling of complex relationships like images and text. However, the nature of the learned relationships is opaque making it difficult to understand precisely what relationships between words and parts of an image are captured, or to predict the effect of an intervention. We illuminate the fine-grained relationships learned by diffusion models by noticing a precise relationship between diffusion and information decomposition. Exact expressions for mutual information and conditional mutual information can be written in terms of the denoising model. Furthermore, pointwise estimates can be easily estimated as well, allowing us to ask questions about the relationships between specific images and captions. Decomposing information even further to understand which variables in a high-dimensional space carry information is a long-standing problem. For diffusion models, we show that a natural non-negative decomposition of mutual information emerges, allowing us to quantify informative relationships between words and pixels in an image. We exploit these new relations to measure the compositional understanding of diffusion models, to do unsupervised localization of objects in images, and to measure effects when selectively editing images through prompt interventions.

papers.title: Exploiting Interpretable Capabilities with Concept-Enhanced Diffusion and Prototype Networks
papers.research_question: How can concept information be leveraged to increase interpretability in machine learning models by integrating it into existing architectures to obtain visual concept representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces concept-enhanced methods that incorporate concept information into existing architectures to generate visual concept representations and perform interpretable concept prediction.
papers.conclusion: Concept-enhanced methods successfully incorporate concept information into existing architectures, enabling the generation of concept-based samples or prototypes and interpretable concept prediction without significant performance loss compared to black-box methods.
papers.key_findings:
Concept-Guided Conditional Diffusion can generate images conditioned on both positive and negative concepts, successfully visualizing concept information.
Concept-Guided Prototype Networks can accurately predict binary concepts and generate interpretable prototype patches for each concept class.
The proposed methods achieve concept prediction accuracy close to a black-box oracle while providing interpretability through visual concept representations.
The methods work on real-world datasets (CUB and AwA2) and with various base architectures (DenseNets, ResNets, VGGs).
The expressivity of concepts is exploited, allowing for generations where direct human interpretation is not trivial (e.g., negative concept guidance).
papers.limitation:
The method relies on concept-annotated datasets.
Generating images with diffusion models is computationally expensive.
future_direction: Extend the work to the continuous concept domain.
Use concept-enhanced methods to understand and mitigate data leakage in Concept Bottleneck Models (CBMs).
Use less computationally demanding variations of diffusion models (e.g., latent diffusion).
papers.abstract: Concept-based machine learning methods have increasingly gained importance due to the growing interest in making neural networks interpretable. However, concept annotations are generally challenging to obtain, making it crucial to leverage all their prior knowledge. By creating concept-enriched models that incorporate concept information into existing architectures, we exploit their interpretable capabilities to the fullest extent. In particular, we propose Concept-Guided Conditional Diffusion, which can generate visual representations of concepts, and Concept-Guided Prototype Networks, which can create a concept prototype dataset and leverage it to perform interpretable concept prediction. These results open up new lines of research by exploiting pre-existing information in the quest for rendering machine learning more human-understandable.

papers.title: Disentangled representations via score-based variational autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we learn disentangled representations without explicit supervision by combining diffusion models and variational autoencoders?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SAMI, a method that combines diffusion models and VAEs to learn disentangled representations without supervision, and can extract interpretable latent representations from pre-trained diffusion models.
papers.conclusion: Implicit structural information in diffusion models can be made explicit and interpretable through synergistic combination with a variational autoencoder.
papers.key_findings:
SAMI recovers ground truth generative factors in synthetic data.
It learns factorized, semantic latent dimensions from complex natural images.
It encodes video sequences into latent trajectories that are straighter than those of alternative encoders.
It can extract useful representations from pre-trained diffusion models with minimal additional training.
The probabilistic formulation allows identification of semantically meaningful axes without supervised labels.
papers.abstract: We present the Score-based Autoencoder for Multiscale Inference (SAMI), a method for unsupervised representation learning that combines the theoretical frameworks of diffusion models and VAEs. By unifying their respective evidence lower bounds, SAMI formulates a principled objective that learns representations through score-based guidance of the underlying diffusion process. The resulting representations automatically capture meaningful structure in the data: it recovers ground truth generative factors in our synthetic dataset, learns factorized, semantic latent dimensions from complex natural images, and encodes video sequences into latent trajectories that are straighter than those of alternative encoders, despite training exclusively on static images. Furthermore, SAMI can extract useful representations from pre-trained diffusion models with minimal additional training. Finally, the explicitly probabilistic formulation provides new ways to identify semantically meaningful axes in the absence of supervised labels, and its mathematical exactness allows us to make formal statements about the nature of the learned representation. Overall, these results indicate that implicit structural information in diffusion models can be made explicit and interpretable through synergistic combination with a variational autoencoder.

papers.title: Patterning: The Dual of Interpretability
papers.research_question: What is the dual problem to interpretability? The paper introduces patterning as the dual: given a desired form of generalization, determine what training data leads to it.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces patterning as the dual of interpretability, using susceptibilities to derive data interventions that steer internal structure formation in neural networks, demonstrated in small language models and a synthetic task.
papers.conclusion: Patterning provides a principled approach to steering generalization by inverting the susceptibility relationship, with potential applications to AI alignment and control of internal structure.
papers.key_findings:
Re-weighting training data along the second principal susceptibility direction can accelerate or delay the formation of the induction circuit.
In the parentheses balancing task, patterning can select which algorithm the model learns by targeting the local learning coefficient of each solution.
Susceptibility-guided interventions produce predictable changes in internal structures.
papers.limitation:
Experiments use small models (3M parameters) and simple tasks.
Susceptibility estimation is computationally expensive.
Focus on one-off interventions made at the start of training, not online control.
Theoretical framework assumes infinitesimal perturbations, while practical interventions are finite; understanding when the linear approximation breaks down is important.
Connection between observables and downstream behavior (e.g., safety properties) requires further study.
future_direction: Develop online control (adjusting data distribution dynamically during training).
Scale to larger models and more efficient methods.
Study the connection to safety properties and AI alignment applications.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to understand how neural networks generalize beyond their training data by reverse-engineering their internal structures. We introduce patterning as the dual problem: given a desired form of generalization, determine what training data produces it. Our approach is based on susceptibilities, which measure how posterior expectation values of observables respond to infinitesimal shifts in the data distribution. Inverting this linear response relationship yields the data intervention that steers the model toward a target internal configuration. We demonstrate patterning in a small language model, showing that re-weighting training data along principal susceptibility directions can accelerate or delay the formation of structure, such as the induction circuit. In a synthetic parentheses balancing task where multiple algorithms achieve perfect training accuracy, we show that patterning can select which algorithm the model learns by targeting the local learning coefficient of each solution. These results establish that the same mathematical framework used to read internal structure can be inverted to write it.

papers.title: TIDE : Temporal-Aware Sparse Autoencoders for Interpretable Diffusion Transformers in Image Generation
papers.research_question: How can we extract sparse, interpretable activation features across timesteps in Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) to understand their internal mechanisms and enable controllability?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces TIDE, a temporal-aware sparse autoencoder framework for extracting interpretable features from Diffusion Transformers, revealing hierarchical semantic representations and enabling applications like safe image editing.
papers.conclusion: TIDE provides a sparse, temporally-aware interpretability framework for DiTs, enabling transparent analysis and practical applications like image editing, laying a foundation for more trustworthy and controllable generative systems.
papers.key_findings:
TIDE effectively captures temporally-varying activation patterns in DiTs, improving reconstruction and generalization.
DiTs naturally learn hierarchical semantics (3D structure, object class, fine-grained concepts) during large-scale pre-training.
TIDE maintains generation quality (e.g., FID) while providing interpretable features, with minimal performance degradation.
The method generalizes across different diffusion backbones (SDXL, FLUX-dev).
TIDE enables safe image editing, achieving a low Attack Success Rate on the I2P benchmark.
papers.limitation: Current performance in complex editing scenarios remains limited by sparsity constraints.
future_direction: Explore more flexible sparse mechanisms to improve expressiveness.
papers.abstract: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) are a powerful yet underexplored class of generative models compared to U-Net-based diffusion architectures. We propose TIDE-Temporal-aware sparse autoencoders for Interpretable Diffusion transformErs-a framework designed to extract sparse, interpretable activation features across timesteps in DiTs. TIDE effectively captures temporally-varying representations and reveals that DiTs naturally learn hierarchical semantics (e.g., 3D structure, object class, and fine-grained concepts) during large-scale pretraining. Experiments show that TIDE enhances interpretability and controllability while maintaining reasonable generation quality, enabling applications such as safe image editing and style transfer.

papers.title: A Unified Theory of Sparse Dictionary Learning in Mechanistic Interpretability: Piecewise Biconvexity and Spurious Minima
papers.research_question: Why do sparse dictionary learning (SDL) methods consistently produce polysemantic features, feature absorption, and dead neurons, and what is the theoretical understanding of these phenomena?
papers.core_contribution: Develops a unified theoretical framework for sparse dictionary learning (SDL) that explains failure modes like feature absorption and dead neurons via piecewise biconvex optimization and non-identifiability, and proposes feature anchoring to improve feature recovery.
papers.conclusion: The theoretical framework explains persistent failure modes in SDL methods, and feature anchoring provides an effective, method-agnostic technique to improve feature recovery by reducing underdetermination.
papers.key_findings:
SDL optimization exhibits piecewise biconvex structure, enabling analysis of its landscape.
SDL suffers from non-identifiability, leading to spurious minima that result in polysemantic features.
Feature absorption arises naturally from hierarchical concept structures and corresponds to partial minima.
Feature anchoring, which constrains a subset of features to known directions, significantly improves feature recovery across SDL methods.
Dead neuron resampling helps escape spurious local minima in large language models.
papers.limitation:
Theoretical analysis relies on the Linear Representation Hypothesis, which assumes features are linear directions; this may not hold for all representations.
The synthetic benchmark, while controlled, may not capture all complexities of real-world data.
Feature anchoring requires anchor features, which may be difficult to obtain in some settings.
future_direction: Extending the theory to non-linear representations.
Applying feature anchoring to more domains and real-world tasks.
Integrating anchoring with other SDL improvements and scaling to larger models.
papers.abstract: As AI models achieve remarkable capabilities across diverse domains, understanding what representations they learn and how they encode concepts has become increasingly important for both scientific progress and trustworthy deployment. Recent works in mechanistic interpretability have widely reported that neural networks represent meaningful concepts as linear directions in their representation spaces and often encode diverse concepts in superposition. Various sparse dictionary learning (SDL) methods, including sparse autoencoders, transcoders, and crosscoders, are utilized to address this by training auxiliary models with sparsity constraints to disentangle these superposed concepts into monosemantic features. These methods are the backbone of modern mechanistic interpretability, yet in practice they consistently produce polysemantic features, feature absorption, and dead neurons, with very limited theoretical understanding of why these phenomena occur. Existing theoretical work is limited to tied-weight sparse autoencoders, leaving the broader family of SDL methods without formal grounding. We develop the first unified theoretical framework that casts all major SDL variants as a single piecewise biconvex optimization problem, and characterize its global solution set, non-identifiability, and spurious optima. This analysis yields principled explanations for feature absorption and dead neurons. To expose these pathologies under full ground-truth access, we introduce the Linear Representation Bench. Guided by our theory, we propose feature anchoring, a novel technique that restores SDL identifiability, substantially improving feature recovery across synthetic benchmarks and real neural representations.

papers.title: In search of dispersed memories: Generative diffusion models are associative memory networks
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether generative diffusion models are mathematically equivalent to modern Hopfield networks, and how this equivalence can provide a unified framework for understanding long-term memory.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that the energy function of generative diffusion models trained on discrete patterns is asymptotically identical to that of modern Hopfield networks, and leverages this connection to formulate a generalized framework for understanding long-term memory as a unified continuum of creative generation and memory recall.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates the mathematical equivalence between modern Hopfield networks and a large class of continuous diffusion models, providing a theoretical framework to model different forms of long-term memory as arising from the same learning mechanism in biological and artificial neural systems.
papers.key_findings:
The energy function of diffusion models trained on discrete patterns is asymptotically identical to the energy function of modern Hopfield networks.
This equivalence holds almost exactly in standard numerical implementations for both exact and trained score models.
Diffusion models generalize Hopfield networks by enabling probabilistic recall and encoding of non-discrete, higher-dimensional memory structures.
The same synaptic learning rule (denoising loss) can encode both episodic and semantic memory within a single distributed neural system.
The framework suggests a biological mechanism for memory consolidation via hippocampal replay and bootstrap re-sampling.
papers.limitation:
It is unlikely that biological neural networks implement pure noise-injection dynamics as in diffusion models.
It is unclear how the reverse and forward dynamics of diffusion models can be simultaneously implemented in brain networks.
future_direction: Implementing diffusion model components in a more biologically plausible way, for example by using stochastic differential equations that model feedforward perceptual feature transformations in sensory cortical areas.
Exploring connections with existing predictive coding models of memory.

Investigating how bootstrap re-sampling, potentially corresponding to hippocampal replays, could address the issue that real-world events are experienced only once, which is necessary for forming episodic memories in the proposed framework.
papers.abstract: Uncovering the mechanisms behind long-term memory is one of the most fascinating open problems in neuroscience and artificial intelligence. Artificial associative memory networks have been used to formalize important aspects of biological memory. Generative diffusion models are a type of generative machine learning techniques that have shown great performance in many tasks. Like associative memory systems, these networks define a dynamical system that converges to a set of target states. In this work we show that generative diffusion models can be interpreted as energy-based models and that, when trained on discrete patterns, their energy function is (asymptotically) identical to that of modern Hopfield networks. This equivalence allows us to interpret the supervised training of diffusion models as a synaptic learning process that encodes the associative dynamics of a modern Hopfield network in the weight structure of a deep neural network. Leveraging this connection, we formulate a generalized framework for understanding the formation of long-term memory, where creative generation and memory recall can be seen as parts of a unified continuum.

papers.title: Deconstructing Denoising Diffusion Models for Self-Supervised Learning
papers.research_question: What components of Denoising Diffusion Models are critical for self-supervised representation learning? Is the representation capability gained by denoising or diffusion processes?
papers.core_contribution: A simplified denoising autoencoder (l-DAE) that adds noise in a low-dimensional latent space (using PCA) achieves competitive self-supervised learning performance, showing that the representation capability of diffusion models stems from denoising rather than the diffusion process.
papers.conclusion: l-DAE, which largely resembles the classical Denoising Autoencoder, can perform competitively in self-supervised learning, with the critical component being a low-dimensional latent space on which noise is added.
papers.key_findings:
Removing class-conditioning improves linear probe accuracy (from 57.5% to 62.5%) even though it harms generation quality.
The latent dimension of the tokenizer is crucial; a relatively low dimension (16 or 32) is optimal for representation learning.
Patch-wise tokenizers (V AE, AE, PCA) perform similarly and outperform convolutional V AE; PCA works well without gradient-based training.
Predicting clean data instead of noise degrades accuracy slightly (65.1% to 62.4%).
Using multiple noise levels is beneficial but not essential; a single noise level can achieve decent accuracy (61.5%).
future_direction: Further research on autoencoder-based methods for self-supervised learning.
papers.abstract: In this study, we examine the representation learning abilities of Denoising Diffusion Models (DDM) that were originally purposed for image generation. Our philosophy is to deconstruct a DDM, gradually transforming it into a classical Denoising Autoencoder (DAE). This deconstructive procedure allows us to explore how various components of modern DDMs influence self-supervised representation learning. We observe that only a very few modern components are critical for learning good representations, while many others are nonessential. Our study ultimately arrives at an approach that is highly simplified and to a large extent resembles a classical DAE. We hope our study will rekindle interest in a family of classical methods within the realm of modern self-supervised learning.

papers.title: Mechanistic Knobs in LLMs: Retrieving and Steering High-Order Semantic Features via Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can internal features in Large Language Models be linked to the reliable control of complex, behavior-level semantic attributes in language generation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a Sparse Autoencoder-based framework for retrieving and steering high-order semantic features in LLMs, enabling precise, bidirectional behavior control and identifying the Functional Faithfulness effect where interventions induce coherent shifts across linguistic dimensions.
papers.conclusion: The findings suggest that LLMs internalize deeply integrated representations of high-order concepts, providing a robust mechanistic path for regulating complex AI behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
SAE-based features allow precise steering of personality traits in LLMs, enabling bidirectional control.
The method outperforms Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) in stability and performance, with higher validity rates.
Functional Faithfulness effect is observed where steering on a feature induces systematic behavioral shifts aligned with the target semantic attribute.
Retrieved features are semantically interpretable and causally effective for model behavior regulation.
LLM internal representations of personality traits align with human psychological frameworks, as shown through social intelligence evaluations.
papers.abstract: Recent work in Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) has enabled the identification and intervention of internal features in Large Language Models (LLMs). However, a persistent challenge lies in linking such internal features to the reliable control of complex, behavior-level semantic attributes in language generation. In this paper, we propose a Sparse Autoencoder-based framework for retrieving and steering semantically interpretable internal features associated with high-level linguistic behaviors. Our method employs a contrastive feature retrieval pipeline based on controlled semantic oppositions, combing statistical activation analysis and generation-based validation to distill monosemantic functional features from sparse activation spaces. Using the Big Five personality traits as a case study, we demonstrate that our method enables precise, bidirectional steering of model behavior while maintaining superior stability and performance compared to existing activation steering methods like Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA). We further identify an empirical effect, which we term Functional Faithfulness, whereby intervening on a specific internal feature induces coherent and predictable shifts across multiple linguistic dimensions aligned with the target semantic attribute. Our findings suggest that LLMs internalize deeply integrated representations of high-order concepts, and provide a novel, robust mechanistic path for the regulation of complex AI behaviors.

papers.title: Eliciting Latent Knowledge from Quirky Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we elicit latent knowledge from language models that are finetuned to make systematic errors, using probes on their activations?
papers.core_contribution: Linear probes on middle-layer activations can extract context-independent knowledge from language models finetuned to output untruthfully, enabling elicitation of correct answers despite deceptive outputs.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that context-independent representations of knowledge exist in quirky models, and probing methods can reliably extract truth, informing scalable oversight of capable systems.
papers.key_findings:
Probes trained on truthful contexts generalize to untruthful contexts, indicating context-independent knowledge representations.
The best probing method (logistic regression on contrast pairs) recovers 75% of the performance gap between truthful and untruthful behavior on hard examples.
Mechanistic anomaly detection using Mahalanobis distance can flag untruthful behavior with an average AUROC of 0.95.
Difference-in-means probing directions are more causally implicated in model output and show better robustness to distribution shifts.
Unsupervised methods like CCS and CRC have an inductive bias towards context-independent generalization but achieve lower in-distribution performance.
papers.limitation:
Measurement of difficulty is a significant limitation, as different difficulty metrics are minimally correlated.
Contrast pair activations come from the answer token position, which is out-of-distribution for the finetuning data.
future_direction: Expand on the diversity and representativeness of evaluations by constructing new quirky datasets and models.
Investigate the limits of context-independent representations by varying the number of personas in finetuning.
Characterize the causal mechanisms involved, such as how intervening on knowledge representations affects output.
papers.abstract: Eliciting Latent Knowledge (ELK) aims to find patterns in a capable neural network's activations that robustly track the true state of the world, especially in hard-to-verify cases where the model's output is untrusted. To further ELK research, we introduce 12 datasets and a corresponding suite of "quirky" language models (LMs) that are finetuned to make systematic errors when answering questions if and only if the keyword "Bob" is present in the prompt. We find that, especially in middle layers, linear probes usually report an LM's knowledge independently of what the LM outputs, enabling us to elicit the correct answer despite the model's untruthful output. The best probing method (logistic regression on contrast pairs) recovers 89% of the gap in AUROC between truthful and untruthful contexts, and 75% for questions harder than those used to train the probe. We also find that a mechanistic anomaly detection approach can flag untruthful behavior with 0.95 AUROC. Our results show promise for eliciting reliable knowledge from capable but untrusted models, and facilitates future research empirically investigating ELK methods.

papers.title: Beyond Surface Statistics: Scene Representations in a Latent Diffusion Model
papers.research_question: Does a latent diffusion model create and use an internal representation of simple scene geometry, specifically depth and salient-object/background distinction?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that Stable Diffusion contains linear internal representations of depth and saliency that emerge early in denoising and play a causal role in image synthesis.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that Stable Diffusion learns internal linear representations of scene geometry, providing evidence that generative models can learn more than surface statistics.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes show representations of depth and saliency in LDM's self-attention layers.
These representations appear in early denoising steps, before images are recognizable to humans.
Intervention experiments confirm that these representations have a causal effect on output geometry.
V AE bottleneck has weaker depth representations compared to LDM.
Self-attention layers encode stronger depth information than convolutional layers.
papers.limitation: Inferring depth from corrupted images using external models trained on natural images is challenging, which may affect label quality.
future_direction: Look for representations of other scene attributes such as lighting or texture.
Investigate semantic aspects of scenes, such as sentiment.
papers.abstract: Latent diffusion models (LDMs) exhibit an impressive ability to produce realistic images, yet the inner workings of these models remain mysterious. Even when trained purely on images without explicit depth information, they typically output coherent pictures of 3D scenes. In this work, we investigate a basic interpretability question: does an LDM create and use an internal representation of simple scene geometry? Using linear probes, we find evidence that the internal activations of the LDM encode linear representations of both 3D depth data and a salient-object / background distinction. These representations appear surprisingly early in the denoising process$-$well before a human can easily make sense of the noisy images. Intervention experiments further indicate these representations play a causal role in image synthesis, and may be used for simple high-level editing of an LDM's output. Project page: https://yc015.github.io/scene-representation-diffusion-model/

papers.title: Interpreting the Weight Space of Customized Diffusion Models
papers.research_question: Can we discover interpretable linear subspaces in the weight space of fine-tuned diffusion models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers an interpretable linear subspace (weights2weights) in the weight space of fine-tuned diffusion models, enabling sampling of new models, semantic editing, and single-image inversion.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a paradigm for representing diffusion model weights as a point in a subspace, forming a meta-latent space that enables controllable creation of new models via sampling, editing, and inversion.
papers.key_findings:
Sampling from the weight subspace yields new models encoding novel, realistic identities.
Linear directions in the weight space correspond to semantic edits (e.g., adding a beard) that preserve identity.
Inverting a single image into the subspace encodes a realistic identity, even for out-of-distribution inputs.
The weight subspace generalizes to other visual concepts like dog breeds and car types.
The subspace provides a strong prior that improves single-image inversion over standard fine-tuning.
papers.limitation:
w2w space inherits biases from the data used to discover it, leading to entangled attributes (e.g., gender and facial hair).
The span of w2w space is limited by the models used to create it, struggling to represent complex identities.
papers.abstract: We investigate the space of weights spanned by a large collection of customized diffusion models. We populate this space by creating a dataset of over 60,000 models, each of which is a base model fine-tuned to insert a different person's visual identity. We model the underlying manifold of these weights as a subspace, which we term weights2weights. We demonstrate three immediate applications of this space that result in new diffusion models -- sampling, editing, and inversion. First, sampling a set of weights from this space results in a new model encoding a novel identity. Next, we find linear directions in this space corresponding to semantic edits of the identity (e.g., adding a beard), resulting in a new model with the original identity edited. Finally, we show that inverting a single image into this space encodes a realistic identity into a model, even if the input image is out of distribution (e.g., a painting). We further find that these linear properties of the diffusion model weight space extend to other visual concepts. Our results indicate that the weight space of fine-tuned diffusion models can behave as an interpretable meta-latent space producing new models.

papers.title: Look the Other Way: Designing 'Positive' Molecules with Negative Data via Task Arithmetic
papers.research_question: Can task arithmetic be used to design molecules with desirable properties by training on negative examples and moving in the opposite direction in weight space?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces molecular task arithmetic, a transfer learning strategy that leverages negative data to design molecules with desirable properties, outperforming traditional finetuning on positive data in terms of diversity and success.
papers.conclusion: Molecular task arithmetic is a simple, data-efficient, and effective transfer learning strategy for drug discovery, with the potential to become a standard approach.
papers.key_findings:
Molecular task arithmetic can generate valid molecules and achieve zero-shot de novo design for single- and dual-objective tasks.
MTA designs more diverse and successful molecules than models finetuned on positive data, even without any positive examples.
MTA can extrapolate beyond the property distributions of the training set, unlike supervised finetuning.
In few-shot settings, MTA combined with finetuning increases the number of diverse hits.
MTA can design well-docking molecules (bioactive) starting from poor-docking molecules, and it can be extended to protein design with transformers.
papers.limitation:
Excessive scaling factor λ can lead to model collapse, with validity and success rate dropping.
Extrapolation capacities depend on the design task and the frequency of positive molecules in the pretraining set.
Combining task vectors of conflicting tasks might introduce task collapse.
future_direction: Integration of molecular task arithmetic with reinforcement learning for goal-directed optimization.
papers.abstract: The scarcity of molecules with desirable properties (i.e., `positive' molecules) is an inherent bottleneck for generative molecule design. To sidestep such obstacle, here we propose molecular task arithmetic: training a model on diverse and abundant negative examples to learn 'property directions' - without accessing any positively labeled data - and moving models in the opposite property directions to generate positive molecules. When analyzed on 33 design experiments with distinct molecular entities (small molecules, proteins), model architectures, and scales, molecular task arithmetic generated more diverse and successful designs than models trained on positive molecules in general. Moreover, we employed molecular task arithmetic in dual-objective and few-shot design tasks. We find that molecular task arithmetic can consistently increase the diversity of designs while maintaining desirable complex design properties, such as good docking scores to a protein. With its simplicity, data efficiency, and performance, molecular task arithmetic bears the potential to become the de facto transfer learning strategy for de novo molecule design.

papers.title: Dissecting and Mitigating Diffusion Bias via Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: How can we understand and mitigate social biases in diffusion models by identifying and manipulating the internal decision-making mechanisms (bias features) that causally drive biased outputs?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces DIFFLENS, a mechanistic interpretability framework that identifies intrinsic bias features within diffusion models and enables fine-grained control over bias levels in generated content by directly manipulating these features.
papers.conclusion: The work provides a novel mechanistic interpretability approach to understand and mitigate bias in diffusion models, offering precise control over bias generation and insights into the model's internal decision-making processes.
papers.key_findings:
The paper identifies specific internal features (bias features) within diffusion models that causally drive the generation of biased content.
The proposed DIFFLENS method effectively mitigates social biases (e.g., gender, age, race) in generated images while preserving image quality and semantic coherence.
DIFFLENS allows for precise, fine-grained control over the level of bias in generated outputs by scaling or suppressing the identified bias features.
Different discovered bias features control distinct fine-grained aspects of generation (e.g., hair style for gender).
The method demonstrates effectiveness on both unconditional and conditional diffusion models across multiple social attributes.
papers.limitation:
The definition and evaluation of social bias are complex and inherently challenging, particularly for attributes like race, leading to potential instability in results.
The sparse autoencoder features may not fully align with human-interpretable concepts, as bias attributes are compound concepts that may relate to multiple features.
The approach treats debiased attributes as discrete categories (e.g., male/female), overlooking individuals who do not fit traditional classifications (e.g., non-binary gender or mixed race).
future_direction: Better alignment of sparse autoencoder features with human-interpretable concepts.
Addressing the representation of non-binary and mixed-race individuals in bias mitigation.
papers.abstract: Diffusion models have demonstrated impressive capabilities in synthesizing diverse content. However, despite their high-quality outputs, these models often perpetuate social biases, including those related to gender and race. These biases can potentially contribute to harmful real-world consequences, reinforcing stereotypes and exacerbating inequalities in various social contexts. While existing research on diffusion bias mitigation has predominantly focused on guiding content generation, it often neglects the intrinsic mechanisms within diffusion models that causally drive biased outputs. In this paper, we investigate the internal processes of diffusion models, identifying specific decision-making mechanisms, termed bias features, embedded within the model architecture. By directly manipulating these features, our method precisely isolates and adjusts the elements responsible for bias generation, permitting granular control over the bias levels in the generated content.
